t: Starship Comes Home Today: SpaceX Will Try the First-Ever Catch of Its Ship at About 3:20 p.m.
d: After 14 trips around Earth, Ship 42 is healthy and headed back to Texas, SpaceX says. If the tower’s arms grab it, it would be a first for the rocket built to fly from Pecan Island.
b:
The second half of SpaceX’s big test comes this afternoon. 
 Starship’s upper stage,  Ship 42 , has spent the night circling Earth and is in good health, SpaceX said Saturday morning. If flight controllers give the final go, it will fall back through the atmosphere and try to land in the arms of the launch tower at Starbase, Texas, at about  3:16 to 3:20 p.m. Central , according to SpaceX’s updates on its webcast, as reported by Space.com. 
 No rocket company has ever caught an orbital spaceship this way. 
 Heat shield looks good 
 Engineers inspected the ship’s tiles two ways: with long-range cameras on the ground, and with cameras riding on a few of the Starlink satellites the ship let go on Friday. 
 The heat shield team signed off after reviewing those images, SpaceX spokesperson Dan Huot said on the webcast, saying it is “in a good posture” to come back through the atmosphere and home to the launch site. 
 Overnight, flight controllers chose to skip an early chance to splash down off South America and keep the ship in space for the full flight. “We are one step closer to an eventual return to launch site,” Huot said. 
 What happened to the booster 
 Friday’s launch went up on time at about 4:47 p.m. Central, but the Super Heavy booster didn’t get caught. It headed for the tower, then turned away and came down offshore in the Gulf. 
 On Saturday, Huot said the booster’s guidance system worked as designed: it “detected that the booster was not in the place that it was supposed to be to proceed with a catch, did an automated abort” and headed offshore. SpaceX is still looking for the root cause. [Read Friday’s launch story.](/news/starship-flight-15-launch-today-double-catch/) 
 Why Pecan Island is watching 
 This is the rocket SpaceX plans to fly from the coast at Pecan Island, a site the company calls a “Starship high-rate launch site.” Flying that often only works if the ships come home in one piece. A catch today would be the first proof it can be done from orbit. 
 How to watch 
 SpaceX streams the landing on its website and X account. A final go/no-go call comes shortly before the landing. We’ll update this story with the result. 
 Will you be watching? Tell us in the comments.

t: Kaplan’s Sammy Kershaw Will Walk the CMA Red Carpet Wednesday; His Manager Tells the Times New Music and a Memoir Are Coming
d: A week after he was turned away, the “She Don’t Know She’s Beautiful” singer accepted the CMA’s apology and invitation. His manager says he’s also working on new songs, a book and “lots of touring.”
b:
Kaplan’s own  Sammy Kershaw  is going to the CMA Awards after all, red carpet and all. 
 A week after he told fans the Country Music Association had denied his request to walk the red carpet, Kershaw said he and his wife, Mendy, have accepted the CMA’s invitation to walk it and attend the show. The 60th Annual CMA Awards are  Wednesday, Nov. 18 , at Bridgestone Arena in Nashville, according to the CMA. 
 “After a lot of thought and prayer, Mendy and I have decided to accept the CMA’s invitation to walk the red carpet and attend the awards,” Kershaw wrote in a Nov. 12 Instagram post, as quoted by Us Weekly. 
 What’s next for Sammy 
 The Times asked Kershaw’s team what his hometown should know. His manager,  Billy Holland  of The Holland Group in Nashville, answered in an email Friday. 
 Kershaw “is working on new music, his memoir and lots of touring,” Holland told the Times. 
 “YOU helped make this happen” 
 The dispute started Nov. 5, when Kershaw posted that the CMA had turned down his request to spend a few minutes on the red carpet, calling it “extremely hurtful, embarrassing and very disappointing.” Country stars and thousands of fans spoke up for him, and his classic songs climbed back up the iTunes chart. 
 On Nov. 9 the CMA said it was “deeply sorry anyone felt excluded” and that it was talking with Kershaw’s team. By the end of the week he had accepted. 
 In his Nov. 12 post, Kershaw thanked the people who backed him. “It’s been a week since so many of you began making your voices heard, and the outpouring of love and support has meant more to me than you’ll ever know,” he wrote, as quoted by KALB. 
 “To the thousands of fans and fellow artists who stood beside us, please know that YOU helped make this happen,” he wrote. 
 He said he was thinking of the legends who came before him: “I think about Dolly, Loretta, George Jones, Charley Pride, and so many others who gave their hearts, voices, and lives to country music.” 
 Watch for him Wednesday 
 The show is Wednesday night, Nov. 18, from Nashville. 
 Kaplan, will you be watching for Sammy on the red carpet? Tell us in the comments, and send us your favorite Sammy Kershaw memory at news@thevermiliontimes.com.

t: Delcambre Stuns No. 8 South Plaquemines 19-18 to Advance; Kaplan Gets Vidalia Next Week
d: The 25th-seeded Delcambre won by a single point on the road. Erath, North Vermilion and Vermilion Catholic saw their seasons end in the first round, according to the LHSAA’s official brackets.
b:
Delcambre  is still playing football. 
 The No. 25 seed went on the road and beat No. 8  South Plaquemines 19-18  in the first round of the Division IV Non-Select playoffs, according to the Louisiana High School Athletic Association’s official bracket. One point was the difference between a long bus ride home and a trip to the regional round. 
 It was the only first-round win for a Vermilion Parish team. 
 First-round scores 
   Delcambre 19, South Plaquemines 18  (Division IV Non-Select). Delcambre advances.   Northwest 31, Erath 16  (Division II Non-Select). Erath’s season ends.   Lutcher 55, North Vermilion 14  (Division II Non-Select). North Vermilion’s season ends.   St. John 48, Vermilion Catholic 27  (Division IV Select). Vermilion Catholic’s season ends.  
 Who’s next 
   Delcambre  (No. 25) plays at  No. 9 Grand Lake  in the regional round.   Kaplan  (No. 4, Division III Non-Select), which had a first-round bye, will  host No. 13 Vidalia , which won its first-round game against Lakeside.  
 The regional round is set for  Nov. 19-21 . The LHSAA lists date ranges; schools set the exact kickoff times, and we’ll post them when the brackets do. 
 Send us your photos 
 Were you in the stands in South Plaquemines? Send your photos from the game to news@thevermiliontimes.com and tell us who took them. We’d love to run the best ones, with credit.

t: SpaceX’s 11th Pecan Island Job: A Safety Manager Who Would Be the Launch Site’s Contact for Local First Responders
d: The new listing, posted Friday, puts the hire in charge of safety and environmental programs “at the Starbase, LA launch site,” including spill response, stormwater and air permits, and working with local emergency agencies.
b:
SpaceX posted another job for its planned Pecan Island launch site on Friday afternoon, and this one would put someone in charge of how the site works with the parish’s emergency responders. 
 The listing, for a  Manager, Environmental Health & Safety  in Pecan Island, La., brings the number of SpaceX openings at the site to  11 , according to the company’s job board. 
 What the job does 
 The manager would lead “all environmental, health, and safety programs at the Starbase, LA launch site,” the listing says, and build a team of technicians, specialists and engineers. 
 Among the duties: 
  Running the site’s workplace safety program under federal OSHA standards  Site environmental policies on hazardous and non-hazardous waste,  air permitting ,  spill prevention and response , and  stormwater   Serving as “the main point of contact for local response agencies”  Representing the safety department in site leadership meetings  
 The posting asks for a bachelor’s degree, at least five years of safety and environmental experience and three years in management, and says “Louisiana experience” is preferred. Like other SpaceX jobs, it requires drug testing and the ability to pass an Air Force background check. No salary is listed. 
 Parts of the listing appear to have been carried over from a SpaceX posting in Florida. It says the job requires relocation “if not already local to the Cape Canaveral, FL area” and lists experience with requirements of the FDEP, Florida’s environmental agency, as a plus. 
 Why the first-responder line matters 
 How a launch site would work with local fire and emergency services is an open question in Vermilion Parish. Last month the citizens’ group Vermilion United said SpaceX had verbally promised firefighting equipment if the project hurts the parish’s fire rating, and asked for that promise in writing. [Read that story.](/news/vermilion-united-questions-spacex-deal/) 
 SpaceX already has a  Sr. Manager, Environmental Health & Safety  listing at Pecan Island, first posted Oct. 15, which describes the site as a “Starship high-rate launch site.” The new job is a separate opening one level below it. 
 Every opening so far 
 SpaceX’s 11 Pecan Island listings now cover construction, engineering, environmental permits, safety, communications, materials and data center power. [See the full list](/news/spacex-louisiana-jobs-pecan-island/), which the Times updates as jobs are added or come down. Job seekers can search SpaceX’s careers page by location for Pecan Island. 
 The Times has asked SpaceX when hourly jobs at the site will open and how parish residents can prepare to apply. We will publish the company’s answer when it arrives.

t: Today’s the Day: SpaceX Goes for the First Catch of an Entire Starship, the Rocket Built to Fly From Pecan Island
d: Liftoff from Texas is set for 4:45 p.m. Central. Minutes later SpaceX will try to snatch the 33-engine booster out of the air with its tower’s arms. Then, after a day in orbit, it wants to do the same with the ship.
b:
Update, 5:25 p.m. Friday:  Starship lifted off at about  4:47 p.m. Central . The booster did not get caught: SpaceX called off the tower catch during the booster’s flight back, and it came down in the Gulf instead, according to SpaceX’s live webcast as reported by Space.com. “We’ll dig in to what caused that abort during its flight back to the tower,” SpaceX’s Dan Huot said on the webcast. The ship finished its climb with all six engines and reached space, and SpaceX said it was “go for orbit,” with the 26 Starlink satellites to be released next. If the ship stays healthy overnight, SpaceX will try the first-ever ship catch on  Saturday , in a window the FAA lists from 2:56 to 6:14 p.m. Central. 
 Within the hour, the biggest rocket ever built will light 33 engines on the Texas coast and try something no one has done before. 
 SpaceX’s  Starship Flight 15  is set to lift off from Starbase, Texas, in a 75-minute window that opens at  4:45 p.m. Central  today. Space.com reported Friday afternoon that the Federal Aviation Administration had approved the flight, clearing the last hurdle. The Times has not yet seen the license on the FAA’s website. 
 If it works, SpaceX says, it will be the first complete recovery of an orbital launch system:  both halves  of the rocket caught by the same tower that launched them. That is the trick SpaceX needs to master before it can fly the way it plans to from Pecan Island. 
 First, the catch 
 Liftoff is only the opening act. Here is SpaceX’s plan, from its mission page: 
   The booster.  After pushing the ship toward space, the Super Heavy booster separates, flips around and fires its engines to fly back to Starbase. As it drops beside the launch tower, two giant steel arms (SpaceX calls them “chopsticks”) close around it and hold it in midair. It’s the first catch attempt for the newer, bigger V3 version of the booster. SpaceX has caught three boosters before, and flown two of them again.   The ship.  Starship keeps climbing to about 275 kilometers, around 170 miles up, and releases  26 Starlink satellites . Three of them carry cameras to photograph the ship’s heat shield in orbit so engineers can check it before bringing it home.   A day in space.  The ship then circles Earth about 14 times over more than 22 hours.  
 Saturday afternoon: the homecoming 
 The second act happens tomorrow. The FAA’s air traffic plan lists a reentry window for the ship on  Saturday from 2:56 to 6:14 p.m. Central . If flight controllers confirm the ship is healthy enough to come back, it will fall through the atmosphere at hypersonic speed, glowing behind its tile heat shield, and head for the same tower that caught the booster. 
 If something isn’t right, SpaceX says it has planned safe places to bring the ship down over the ocean instead. 
 Why Vermilion Parish should watch 
 This is the rocket SpaceX wants to fly from the coast at Pecan Island. One of the company’s Louisiana job listings calls the Pecan Island site a “Starship high-rate launch site,” and the state says launches there are planned to begin in 2029. [Here’s what we know about Starbase Louisiana.](/news/starbase-louisiana-what-we-know/) 
 High-rate is the key word. A rocket that comes back in one piece can be refueled and flown again in days instead of rebuilt over months. That is how SpaceX talks about hundreds of launches a year, and it is why a full catch tonight and tomorrow matters to the people who will live next to the next Starbase. 
 How to watch 
 Space.com reports SpaceX moved the start of its live webcast up to about  3:58 p.m. Central , on its website and X account. The FAA’s plan lists  Saturday at the same time  as a backup launch date if today’s attempt is called off. 
 Launch times and the countdown are also on the Times’ [Starbase Watch page](/starbase/#live). We’ll update this story with how it went.

t: Abbeville’s Downtown Street Project Wins a National Federal Highway Award, the First in a New ‘Putting Families First’ Category
d: The Federal Highway Administration named the city’s downtown revival the national winner of its new family-focused innovation award. The prize carries no money, but it puts Abbeville in front of road builders across the country.
b:
The work that remade downtown Abbeville’s streets has earned the city a national title. 
 The Federal Highway Administration has named the  City of Abbeville  the national winner of its  Putting Families First Innovation Award , a category added this year to the agency’s Build a Better Mousetrap competition. Abbeville is the first city to win it. The winning entry was the city’s “Downtown Revival Abbeville Street Improvement Project.” 
 FHWA’s winners page says the city “created a safer community-centered downtown environment through extensive public engagement and multimodal transportation planning.” 
 What the contest is 
 Build a Better Mousetrap is run by FHWA’s Center for Local Aid Support. It honors practical ideas from local road departments, cities and tribes, from homemade tools to new ways of planning. Entries reach the national round through each state’s Local Technical Assistance Program, and Louisiana’s program picked Abbeville as the state’s entry. 
 This year’s other national winners were public works crews and counties in New Hampshire, California, New York and Iowa, honored for a culvert-steaming truck, an AI street inventory, a snow-fence pole puller and a GPS survey rig. According to the city, FHWA weighed more than 100 entries from the 2025 and 2026 contest years before choosing. 
 What Abbeville built 
 The city says the project started as a plan to fix aging streets and safety problems in the Historic Main Street District, then grew into something bigger. Before anything permanent went in, the city held community meetings, ran traffic studies and set up a temporary demonstration so residents could try the changes and weigh in. 
 According to the city, the finished work includes: 
  Better pedestrian crossings and safer intersections  Traffic-calming features  Room for bicycles  New sidewalks  Decorative touches that reflect Abbeville’s history and culture  
 The goal, the city says, was a downtown that works for people “of all ages and abilities” and helps local businesses and events. 
 No money, but a bigger stage 
 The award does not come with any funding, the city says, but it brings national attention that could help with future grant applications and partnerships. 
 LeJeune, the city’s media and communications coordinator, prepared the entry. Next month he will walk transportation officials through the project in one of FHWA’s Innovation Exchange webinars. In March he takes it to Baton Rouge for the 2027 Louisiana Transportation Conference (March 7-10), where the state’s LTAP center plans to give Abbeville its national plaque. 
 The webinar “is an opportunity to share our project with transportation professionals and agencies from across the country, discuss what worked, and hopefully give other communities ideas they can use in their own projects,” LeJeune told the Times in an email. 
 He also credited Courtney Dupre, program manager for the state’s LTAP, with making sure the project was entered before the deadline. “It’s pretty exciting to see how far this project has gone,” he said. 
 Two other Louisiana projects were in this year’s state lineup: Calcasieu Parish’s flood warning system, built on over 100 gauges that track rain and water levels, and a St. Charles Parish repair method for the timber piles under a water intake in Luling.

t: Abbeville Honors Marion Bessard Jr. and Donald Ray Shelvin, the First Black Men to Join Its National Guard Unit
d: In 1974 the two Abbeville High students enlisted together in the city’s Louisiana Army National Guard battalion. On Veterans Day, Mayor Anita Levy’s proclamation called them pioneers of the unit’s integration.
b:
Fifty-two years after they signed up together, two Abbeville men have been honored by their hometown for opening the door for others. 
 The City of Abbeville recognized  Marion J. Bessard Jr.  and  Donald Ray Shelvin  at a Veterans Day service at Macedonia Baptist Church on Wednesday, Nov. 11. Mayor Anita Levy’s proclamation, issued with the City Council, honors them as the first African American men to enlist in the Abbeville-based  2nd Battalion, 156th Infantry Regiment of the Louisiana Army National Guard , in 1974. 
 The proclamation calls that “a significant milestone in the integration of the local military unit” and “an important chapter in the history of Abbeville and Vermilion Parish.” 
 Two classmates, one decision 
 Both men were Abbeville High School students when they answered the call to serve together, according to the proclamation. Bessard graduated from Abbeville High in 1974. 
 They were recruited by Chief Warrant Officer 4 D. A. LeBlanc, the city’s proclamation says, and went through basic training at  Fort Leonard Wood, Missouri . They joined at a time when the country’s armed forces were still working through integration, and the proclamation says their willingness to serve then “demonstrated courage, determination, and a commitment to overcoming barriers, helping open doors for future generations of service members.” 
 The mayor and council recognized both men “for their military service, their pioneering roles in the integration of the Abbeville-based Louisiana Army National Guard unit, and their lasting contributions to the history of Abbeville and Vermilion Parish.” 
 [[img: /img/photos/abbeville-veterans-mayor-levy-macedonia.jpg | Mayor Anita Levy, in a navy blazer with her name embroidered on it, stands with three men in front of the pulpit at Macedonia Baptist Church, an American flag behind them | Mayor Anita Levy, second from left, at the Nov. 11 Veterans Day service at Macedonia Baptist Church, where the city honored Marion J. Bessard Jr. and Donald Ray Shelvin. Photo: City of Abbeville]] 
 “Trailblazers” 
 The recognition was spearheaded by  Councilman Terry Broussard , who represents District D. The city says he gathered the history of the two men’s service and brought it to light. 
 “These two men are trailblazers who answered the call to serve our country while helping pave the way for future generations of African Americans in military service,” Broussard said in a statement provided by the city. 
 “Their courage, dedication, and service are an important part of Abbeville’s history,” he said. “As a community, we owe them a debt of gratitude, and it is our responsibility to honor their contributions and carry their legacy forward.” 
 The proclamation closes by thanking the two veterans for their service “to our state and nation, and for the legacy they have established for our community and future generations.” 
 Do you know a Vermilion Parish veteran whose story should be told? Send it to news@thevermiliontimes.com.

t: Gueydan Mayor’s Runoff: Online Voter Registration Closes Nov. 21, Early Voting Starts Nov. 28
d: Jason Suire and Efrem “Zim” Livingston are the only names on Vermilion Parish’s Dec. 12 ballot, according to the Secretary of State. Here are the dates every Gueydan voter needs.
b:
Gueydan will choose its next mayor on  Saturday, Dec. 12 , and the clock is already running for anyone who still needs to register. 
 The race between aldermen  Jason Suire  and  Efrem “Zim” Livingston  is the only contest listed for Vermilion Parish on the Dec. 12 ballot, according to the Louisiana Secretary of State’s candidate list. That means only Gueydan voters have a race to decide next month. 
 The dates 
 These come from the Secretary of State’s calendar for the Dec. 12 election: 
   Thursday, Nov. 12:  the deadline to register in person, by mail or at an OMV office has passed.   Saturday, Nov. 21:  last day to register  online  through the state’s GeauxVote system.   Saturday, Nov. 28 to Saturday, Dec. 5:  early voting, 8:30 a.m. to 6 p.m. daily, except Sunday, Nov. 29.   Tuesday, Dec. 8, 4:30 p.m.:  deadline to request an absentee (mail) ballot, other than military and overseas voters. Requests can be made online through the state’s Voter Portal or in writing to the parish Registrar of Voters.   Friday, Dec. 11, 4:30 p.m.:  the registrar must have your completed absentee ballot in hand by then.   Saturday, Dec. 12:  election day. Polls are open from 7 a.m. to 8 p.m.  
 The state’s Voter Portal, at voterportal.sos.la.gov, shows each voter’s registration status, polling place, early voting site and sample ballot. 
 How we got here 
 No candidate won a majority on Nov. 3. Suire led with 133 votes (36%), Livingston had 121 (32.8%) and Jeffrey Lamson had 115 (31.2%), according to unofficial returns. Just 18 votes separated first place from third. The Secretary of State’s results page still listed the Nov. 3 returns as unofficial on Friday morning. 
 The state’s qualifying records list Suire as a Republican and Livingston as a Democrat. Both qualified for the race in early August. 
 What’s on the town’s plate 
 Whoever wins will inherit the budget the current board is now writing. Gueydan has a public hearing on its amended 2026 budget and its proposed 2027 budget set for  Tuesday, Dec. 1, at 5:45 p.m.  at City Hall, 11 days before the runoff, with final votes planned at the 6 p.m. council meeting that follows. Both candidates sit on that board. [Read our story on the town’s budget and utility fund transfers.](/news/gueydan-budget-hearing-utility-transfers-fire-station/) 
 The Vermilion Times will post results from Gueydan on election night. Candidates who want to tell voters about their plans can reach the newsroom at news@thevermiliontimes.com.

t: SpaceX’s First Big Louisiana Permit Doesn’t Say ‘Launch’: It’s Called the ‘Coastal Infrastructure Improvement Project’
d: State records show SpaceX applied in September to build a Gulf wharf at Freshwater City, barge docks, a 15.75-mile heavy-haul road with a 1.5-mile bridge, and to dredge area canals, touching nearly 888 acres of wetlands and water bottoms. Work would run from 2027 to 2032.
b:
The first major permit SpaceX has filed for its Vermilion Parish project is not called Starbase Louisiana, and it never mentions rockets or launches. 
 State records reviewed by The Vermilion Times show Space Exploration Technologies Corp. applied on Sept. 25 for a coastal use permit for the  ”Southwest Louisiana Coastal Infrastructure Improvement Project.”  The joint application went to the Louisiana Department of Conservation and Energy and the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers’ New Orleans District, which both must approve work in the coastal zone. 
 The application describes a cargo operation: a Gulf wharf, barge docks, a heavy-haul road and canal dredging, all at the southern tip of the parish near Pecan Island. In its 12 pages, the only “launch” is the existing  Freshwater City Boat Launch , which the plan says it will avoid. “Rocket” appears only in SpaceX’s own mailing address, 1 Rocket Road in Starbase, Texas. 
 The FAA told the Times on Thursday that SpaceX has not yet applied for the federal review needed to launch Starship from Louisiana. [Read that story.](/news/faa-spacex-no-application-starship-louisiana/) 
 [[img: /img/photos/spacex-pecan-island-road-map.jpg | Map of southern Vermilion Parish showing the northern end of SpaceX’s proposed heavy-haul road near LA 82 and its southern end at a Gulf wharf site beside the Freshwater Bayou Canal near the coast | The end points of SpaceX’s proposed heavy-haul road, from its coastal permit application. The dashed line shows general direction only; the 15.75-mile route and its 8,110-foot bridge have not been made public. Map: The Vermilion Times; imagery: USGS The National Map.]] 
 What SpaceX wants to build 
 According to the application: 
   A Gulf wharf  for “moderate-draft” ships, just below the Corps’ Freshwater City Lock on the Freshwater Bayou Channel, with a temporary laydown yard north of the lock.   Inland wharves  along existing channels where barges can reach the Intracoastal Waterway and Freshwater Bayou.   A heavy-haul access road  about  15.75 miles long , running from LA 82 south to the wharves, mostly on an earthen berm through marsh, with an  8,110-foot elevated bridge  (about 1.5 miles) to keep boat traffic moving on the Humble Canal.   Maintenance dredging  of the Humble Canal, Freshwater Bayou and nearby channels so vessels can reach the docks.  
 The site is at the end of LA 3147, Freshwater City Road. The application says the work is privately funded. 
 Why, in SpaceX’s words 
 The project is needed for year-round cargo transfer between Gulf ships that need “lock-free access to the Gulf of America,” Intracoastal barges and a heavy-haul road, the filing says, for oversized, overweight and bulk cargo that cannot practically move on existing public roads or through the parish’s existing shallow-draft facilities. The application does not say what the cargo is. 
 How big it is 
 The numbers in the application: 
   887.67 acres  of wetlands and water bottoms filled or dug out.   5.19 million cubic yards  of excavation across 565 acres, and  11.19 million cubic yards  of fill across 540 acres.  About  125,000 cubic yards of concrete ,  215,000 cubic yards of asphalt ,  1.3 million cubic yards of crushed stone or gravel  and  1.7 million cubic yards of sand .   Proposed schedule:  start March 1, 2027; finish Sept. 1, 2032.  
 Other sites considered 
 SpaceX’s engineers evaluated four Gulf wharf sites in Vermilion and Cameron parishes, four road routes and three dredging approaches, according to the filing. Other wharf sites were ruled out for lack of road access, utilities, waterway connections or room, and one sat inside the Rockefeller Wildlife Refuge. The Freshwater City site was picked as the least damaging practical choice because it already has commercial development and direct Gulf access, the application says. Widening existing highways was rejected because they cannot carry the loads, and a fully elevated causeway was called too expensive.

t: FAA Tells the Times: SpaceX Has Not Applied to Launch Starship From Louisiana
d: The federal agency that must approve any launch from Pecan Island says it has no SpaceX application to review yet. Next week’s Starship hearings are about the Texas site only, the FAA said.
b:
SpaceX has not yet asked the Federal Aviation Administration to review rocket launches from Vermilion Parish, the agency told The Vermilion Times on Thursday. 
 “SpaceX has not submitted an application for the FAA to evaluate proposed Starship operations in Louisiana,” the FAA said in a statement emailed in response to the Times’ questions. 
 The FAA is the federal agency that licenses commercial rocket launches. Before Starship can fly from Pecan Island, the agency has to evaluate the proposed operations, and the FAA’s answer means that process has not started. 
 Next week’s hearings are about Texas 
 The Times asked whether SpaceX’s Louisiana site is part of the FAA’s current review of Starship operations, which includes five online public meetings Nov. 17-19 and a comment period that runs through Dec. 7. That review would allow up to 456 launches a year from SpaceX’s Boca Chica site. [Read about it.](/news/faa-starbase-texas-456-launches-gulf-landings-virtual-hearings/) 
 The answer was no. The meetings “relate to that facility only,” the FAA said, referring to the Texas launch site. 
 The agency also said it plans to hold in-person meetings once a draft environmental study for the Texas expansion is ready for public review. The materials for next week’s online meetings are posted on the  FAA’s project page . 
 Still unanswered 
 The FAA’s statement did not address the Times’ questions about whether the Texas plan’s Gulf landing and splashdown zones include waters off Louisiana, or whether the review will consider Louisiana’s coastal communities and commercial fishing. The Times will keep asking. 
 The timeline so far 
 Louisiana Economic Development says construction at the Vermilion Parish site should begin by the end of 2027, with the first launch targeted as soon as 2029. LED’s project page says the project “will go through all applicable environmental, wetlands, natural resource and launch-related reviews.” 
 The Texas review shows what that process looks like once it starts: public meetings and a formal comment period. The Times will report it as soon as SpaceX files for Louisiana. 
 Follow every development on the Times’ [Starbase Watch page](/starbase/).

t: Trump Says the U.S. Doesn’t Need a Deal With Iran: ‘We’ve Got Their Strait.’ Oil Ticks Up as Gulf Coast Gas Prices Fall
d: The president’s post on Thursday pushed crude higher for a while after weeks of hopes for a settlement. At the pump, Gulf Coast regular gasoline averaged $3.48 a gallon this week, down 15 cents, but still 88 cents above a year ago.
b:
President Donald Trump said Thursday that the United States no longer needs a deal with Iran, a turn from days of signals that talks to end the U.S.-Iran war were moving forward. 
 “We don’t need a deal with Iran. Those days have long since passed,” Trump wrote on Truth Social, according to CNBC and Bloomberg News. “We’ve got their money, Hundreds of Billions of Dollars, and we’ve got their Strait!” 
 Earlier this week he had said more military action did not seem needed “at this point,” and on Sunday he called new attacks on Iran “highly unlikely” as talks went on, CNBC reported. 
 Oil moves, then settles 
 Brent crude, the global benchmark, jumped on the post before giving back some of the gain, Bloomberg reported. By Thursday morning it was up about half a percent, near $93.30 a barrel. U.S. crude was roughly flat, near $86, according to CNBC. 
 Oil has had a wild year. Brent is up more than 50% since January but has dropped sharply this month as traders priced in a possible end to the fighting, Bloomberg reported, and U.S. crude is down about 16% in November, according to CNBC. One analyst told CNBC the market “may have gotten ahead of itself” in betting on peace. 
 What’s happening in the Gulf 
 The two sides still disagree on Iran’s nuclear program, its frozen money and the U.S. naval blockade, Bloomberg reported. Iran’s semi-official ISNA news agency said two loaded supertankers were stopped by explosions on Nov. 11 while using what Iran called an “unauthorized” route through the Strait of Hormuz. 
 A senior Iranian security official, Mohsen Rezaee, said in an interview with the Al Mayadeen network that Iran would not give up “a single atom” of its enriched nuclear material, according to Bloomberg. 
 What it means at the pump here 
 Gas prices along the Gulf Coast have been falling with crude. Regular gasoline in the Gulf Coast region, which includes Louisiana, averaged  $3.48 a gallon  on Nov. 9, down about 15 cents from the week before, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration. That is still about 88 cents higher than a year ago. The national average was just under $4. 
 Diesel, which farmers, fishermen and truckers in the parish depend on, averaged  $5.74 a gallon  in the Gulf Coast region, down 17 cents in a week but about $2.31 above last year, the agency reported. 
 The agency’s next weekly prices come out Tuesday, Nov. 17. A lasting jump in crude after Thursday’s post would show up there first.

t: Musk: ‘Starbase, Louisiana Will Unlock That Future’
d: In a statement the state posted on its SpaceX project page, Elon Musk calls the planned Vermilion Parish spaceport something that “has only existed in science fiction.” Here is his full statement and what the state says will be built.
b:
Elon Musk has a big promise for Vermilion Parish. 
 “We’re preparing to build a spaceport that, until now, has only existed in science fiction,” the SpaceX CEO said. 
 “SpaceX was founded to bring about a future where humans are out exploring amongst the stars,” Musk said, “which will only be possible when we make going to space as routine as flying on an airplane.” 
  ”Starbase, Louisiana will unlock that future.”  
 The statement appears on Louisiana Economic Development’s official page for the project, alongside one from Gov. Jeff Landry thanking SpaceX “for believing in Louisiana.” 
 What the state says will be built 
 According to LED’s page: 
   The largest spaceport in the world,  built to handle thousands of launches a year.   Five launch complexes, each with two pads,  at full buildout, plus propellant storage, a plant to make rocket propellant, and employee housing.   Construction starting by the end of 2027,  with the first launch targeted as soon as  2029 .   3,000 direct jobs  over 10 years at an average salary of  $92,600 , and about 8,100 indirect jobs.   $20 million up front and at least $25 million a year for 25 years  to local taxing bodies under the payment-in-lieu-of-taxes deal, more than $825 million in all.   A $25 million gift  from SpaceX to the Community Foundation of Acadiana.  
 What is still open 
 The same page says road and bridge needs are still being studied, with improvements to LA 82 under review and “some cost sharing” expected between the state and SpaceX. It says SpaceX will pay for new power generation and grid upgrades so current electric customers are not hurt, and that the project still needs its environmental, wetlands and launch approvals. 
 Confidential state records published this week also showed an early LED briefing listing “a new city in Vermilion Parish” among the needs to win the project. The Times has asked LED about it. [Read that story.](/news/spacex-new-city-vermilion-parish-project-osprey-records/) 
 Follow every development on the Times’ [Starbase Watch page](/starbase/).

t: State’s Secret SpaceX Plan Listed ‘a New City in Vermilion Parish,’ Records Show
d: A March briefing by Louisiana Economic Development, code-named Project Osprey, named a new city among the things needed to win SpaceX. A month later the line was gone. The Times has asked the state what it meant and whether residents would get a say.
b:
Months before SpaceX’s Aug. 25 announcement in downtown Abbeville, the state’s economic development agency listed something bigger than a launch site among its needs to land the company: a new city in Vermilion Parish. 
 That is according to state records published Wednesday by the Gulf States Newsroom, the public radio partnership that includes New Orleans’ WWNO. The documents are posted online, and much of what is in them is blacked out. 
 What the records say 
 A March 12, 2026 briefing by Louisiana Economic Development, marked highly confidential and code-named  ”Project Osprey,”  lists “the construction of a new city in Vermilion Parish” among the “anticipated needs to win” what it calls a $100 billion spaceport, the newsroom reported. 
 The briefing does not say who would run such a city or what role SpaceX would have, and nearly everything beneath that line is redacted, according to the report. A newer version of the briefing from April  no longer mentions a new city , and the records do not explain why. 
 Other details the newsroom found in the records: 
   Size of the first phase:  $20 billion or more in investment, perhaps as much as $50 billion, and 3,000 or more jobs, described as “the world’s largest launch site.”   The land:  the main and backup sites were owned by ExxonMobil and bound by a 100-year lease belonging to the Vermilion Duck Hunting Club.   A Texas comparison:  an LED official sent around a presentation about Starbase, Texas, SpaceX’s company town, which incorporated as a city in May 2025 after a vote of 212 to 6 and chose a SpaceX vice president to be its mayor. The newsroom noted the Louisiana records do not explicitly say the state meant to copy Starbase.   A “whole-of-government” meeting  on July 9 listed 27 expected attendees, including the Army Corps of Engineers, LED, the state transportation and coastal agencies, three electric cooperatives (SLEMCO, Jeff Davis Electric and 1803 Electric), One Acadiana, an engineering firm and a law firm.  
 LED, SpaceX and Gov. Jeff Landry’s office did not answer the newsroom’s questions about the records, it reported. 
 Why it matters here 
 A new city would change who governs land near the launch site and who sets the rules there. In Texas, Starbase became its own city with a SpaceX vice president as mayor. 
 Nothing in the records published so far shows that a city is being formed in Vermilion Parish, and the April briefing dropped the idea from its list without explanation. 
 What the state says publicly 
 Louisiana Economic Development’s own public page on the project does not mention a city. It does say that at full buildout, the site is expected to include  employee housing , along with five launch complexes with two pads each, propellant storage and a plant to make rocket propellant. LED’s page says construction should begin by the end of 2027, with the first launch targeted as soon as 2029. 
 The records add to questions already being raised at home. Parish residents and a nonprofit have sued the Police Jury and the parish’s industrial development board, saying the SpaceX tax deal was approved in violation of the Open Meetings Law. [Read our coverage of the lawsuit.](/news/residents-sue-to-void-spacex-tax-deal/) 
 What we asked the state 
 On Thursday, the Times asked Louisiana Economic Development what “the construction of a new city in Vermilion Parish” meant, whether it is still being discussed, why it was dropped from the April briefing, and whether residents or the Police Jury would get a public say. We will update this story with LED’s answer. 
  The records were first reported by Drew Hawkins of WWNO and the Gulf States Newsroom. Their full report is linked in the sources below.  
 Follow every development on the Times’ [Starbase Watch page](/starbase/).

t: New SpaceX Job Says Starship Will Be Built in Louisiana, With Staff Moving Here in Early 2027
d: A director’s listing describes Starship production at the Pecan Island site and says the hire relocates to Louisiana early next year. A second new posting, for a lawyer to win power approvals for SpaceX data centers, is also listed at Pecan Island. That makes 10 openings.
b:
SpaceX plans to build Starship rockets in Vermilion Parish, not just launch them, and it expects to start moving people here early next year, according to a job the company posted Tuesday night. 
 The listing, for a  Director of Materials Management  at “our new Louisiana site,” is the clearest statement yet in SpaceX’s own words about what Starbase Louisiana will be. It also gives the first timeline we have seen from the company for staff arriving in the parish. 
 “Starship production” at Pecan Island 
 The director would run the warehouse and parts operation “in support of Starship production” at the Louisiana site, the posting says. That means receiving and tracking everything from huge rocket sections and engine hardware to electronics and heat-shield parts, and getting it to the production lines on time. 
 The posting describes a site that will grow: 
  The director will “build the organization, systems, and material flow required for a new site,” then expand them “as production rate increases.”  The job covers “new buildings and production lines” and “campus planning.”  The hire will lead managers, supervisors, analysts and  warehouse associates across shifts , both hourly and salaried workers.  
 It is the first Pecan Island listing the Times has seen that mentions hourly warehouse workers; every earlier opening was a senior professional role. The listing does not say how many people the team will have. 
 Moving to Louisiana in early 2027 
 The job starts at Starbase, Texas, near Brownsville. “At that time, relocation to Louisiana will be required,” the posting says of  early 2027 . 
 It is the first SpaceX listing we have seen that puts a date on when a Pecan Island hire is expected to work in Louisiana. 
 A lawyer for data center power 
 The second new posting,  Sr. Regulatory Counsel, Data Center Power & Utilities , is also listed at Pecan Island. The lawyer would win the approvals SpaceX needs to draw “large amounts of power” for its data center and computing sites, working with utility regulators, grid operators and power companies on hookups, rates and special contracts. 
 The posting talks about SpaceX’s data center sites in general and  does not say a data center is planned at Pecan Island . It does list the job there. Earlier this month, SpaceX also posted an air-permit job covering on-site power plants in Louisiana and Texas. [Read about that listing.](/news/spacex-pecan-island-jobs-wetlands-air-permits/) 
 In Louisiana, large utility arrangements generally go before the state Public Service Commission. 
 Neither posting lists a salary. The director job asks for a bachelor’s degree, at least five years in fields such as manufacturing or supply chain, and four years leading managers. The counsel job asks for a law degree and eight years of utility or energy law. 
 All 10 Pecan Island openings 
 As of Wednesday morning, SpaceX lists these jobs at Pecan Island: 
   Director, Materials Management  (Starbase Infrastructure, Louisiana)  (new Nov. 10)    Sr. Regulatory Counsel, Data Center Power & Utilities   (new Nov. 10)   Sr. Construction Project Manager (Starship Infrastructure, Louisiana)  Civil Engineer, Land Development (Starbase Infrastructure, Louisiana)  Sr. Construction Safety Engineer  Sr. Environmental Engineer  Sr. Environmental Engineer, Wetlands & Regulatory Compliance  Sr. Environmental Regulatory Engineer, Air Permitting  Sr. Manager, Environmental Health & Safety  Communications Lead  
 SpaceX does not say when the warehouse and production jobs will open to applicants. The Times checks the board every day; the live count is on our [Starbase Watch page](/starbase/#lv-jobs-h), and our [running list](/news/spacex-louisiana-jobs-pecan-island/) has every opening so far.

t: Abbey Players Open ‘Joseph and the Amazing Technicolor Dreamcoat’ Friday in Downtown Abbeville
d: Abbeville’s community theater stages the family musical over two weekends, Nov. 13-22, at its State Street theater. Tickets are $20. Here are the showtimes, the cast and how to get tickets.
b:
The coat of many colors comes to downtown Abbeville this weekend. 
 The Abbey Players, the parish’s community theater since 1976, open  Joseph and the Amazing Technicolor Dreamcoat  on  Friday, Nov. 13 , at their theater at 200 S. State St. The show runs two weekends and closes Sunday, Nov. 22, according to the troupe’s ticket listing. 
 Showtimes 
   Friday, Nov. 13:  7 p.m.   Saturday, Nov. 14:  7 p.m.   Sunday, Nov. 15:  2 p.m. matinee   Friday, Nov. 20:  7 p.m.   Saturday, Nov. 21:  7 p.m.   Sunday, Nov. 22:  2 p.m. matinee  
  Tickets are $20  for every seat, the Abbey Players said, and are sold online through the  Abbey Players website , which links to the troupe’s ticketing page. 
 The show 
  Joseph  is the Andrew Lloyd Webber and Tim Rice musical built on the Bible story of Joseph, Jacob’s favorite son, and the coat that made his eleven brothers jealous. The whole story is sung, with a Narrator guiding the audience as Joseph is sold by his brothers, lands in an Egyptian prison, reads dreams for a Pharaoh styled after Elvis, and finally saves Egypt from famine and reunites with his family. 
 The theater bills it as a family musical. 
 Who’s in it 
  Mitchell Prudhomme  plays Joseph and  Stacy Cueva  is the Narrator, the troupe’s board of directors told the Times in an email. 
   Director:  Hollie Thorne   Assistant director:  Shea Best   Music director:  Alexa Theriot   Choreographer:  Dr. Malani Hoffpauir  
 The cast includes performers from across Acadiana, and 10 couples are in the show together, the board said. 
 All volunteers 
 Nobody at the Abbey Players is paid. Every production, this one included, is put on by volunteers who do it “for the love of theater and entertaining others,” the board wrote. “We can’t wait to entertain you!” 
 About the Abbey Players 
 The troupe calls itself “South Louisiana Community Theater Since 1976,” and says its mission is to give local performers a welcoming place to create and to entertain Abbeville and the rest of Acadiana. Local actors, singers and volunteers make up its casts and crews, and the group posts auditions, volunteer sign-ups and its full season on its website.

t: SpaceX Will Try to Catch Both Halves of Starship on Friday, the Rocket It Plans to Fly From Pecan Island
d: Starship Flight 15 could launch from Texas as soon as Friday at 4:45 p.m. Central. SpaceX says it would be the first time the booster and the ship both come back to the tower, the kind of reuse a high-rate site like Starbase Louisiana depends on.
b:
Update, Friday morning:  The FAA’s national air traffic plan for Friday lists Starship Flight 15 with a launch window of  4:45 to 6:40 p.m. Central  today and a backup window at the same time Saturday. It also lists a separate reentry window for the ship on  Saturday, from 2:56 to 6:14 p.m. Central , with the same window Sunday as a backup. As of Friday morning, the Times could not find a published FAA license for this flight, and SpaceX still lists it as pending regulatory approval. 
 The rocket SpaceX wants to launch from Pecan Island faces its biggest test yet this week. 
 SpaceX says Starship’s 15th flight could lift off from Starbase, Texas, as soon as  Friday, Nov. 13 , in a 75-minute window opening at  4:45 p.m. Central . The launch still needs regulatory approval, and the company warns the date is likely to move. 
 What makes this one different 
 For the first time, SpaceX plans to bring  both  stages back to the launch tower and catch them in its mechanical arms: the Super Heavy booster minutes after liftoff, and the Starship upper stage after almost a full day in orbit. If both catches work, the company says, it would be the first complete recovery of an orbital launch system. 
 Here is the plan, according to SpaceX’s flight page: 
   The booster  separates, turns around and flies back for a catch. It is the first catch try for the newer V3 version of Super Heavy. SpaceX has caught three earlier boosters, and two of those flew again.   The ship  climbs to about 275 kilometers (roughly 170 miles), releases 26 of SpaceX’s newest Starlink satellites, and circles Earth about 14 times over more than 22 hours.   The homecoming:  Starship heads back to Texas for a catch only if flight controllers confirm the systems it needs for reentry and landing are healthy. If not, SpaceX says it has planned safe places to bring it down over the ocean.  
 Three of the satellites carry cameras to photograph Starship’s heat shield in orbit, so engineers can check it before committing to a return. The ship also carries heat-shield changes from the last flight, including extra tile fasteners and a curved tile design meant to cut heating in the gaps. 
 Why it matters in Vermilion Parish 
 Catching and quickly reflying both stages is the whole idea behind Starship, and behind the kind of launch site SpaceX is planning near Pecan Island. One of the company’s Louisiana job listings describes the site as a “Starship high-rate launch site.” [See every Louisiana opening.](/news/spacex-louisiana-jobs-pecan-island/) 
 A rocket that comes home in one piece can fly again within days instead of being rebuilt. That is how SpaceX can talk about hundreds of launches a year: on Tuesday the FAA published its plan to study up to 456 Starship launches a year from the Texas site alone. [Read that story.](/news/faa-starbase-texas-456-launches-gulf-landings-virtual-hearings/) 
 How to watch 
 SpaceX will stream the flight on its website and its X account, starting about 30 minutes before liftoff. The company says coverage could run through the ship’s catch the next day, with hours of live video from orbit. 
 Launch times and the countdown are also on the Times’ [Starbase Watch page](/starbase/#live), which updates on its own.

t: Buc-ee’s Breaks Ground in Lafayette, Its Closest Store to Vermilion Parish, With a February 2028 Target
d: The $82 million travel center at I-10 and Louisiana Avenue will have 120 gas pumps, about 700 parking spaces and boudin on the menu. Lafayette’s economic development agency says it will support more than 300 jobs.
b:
The beaver is finally on its way to Acadiana. Buc-ee’s held a groundbreaking Monday for a travel center on the north side of Lafayette, about 20 miles as the crow flies from Abbeville. When it opens, it will be the closest Buc-ee’s to Vermilion Parish by a long way. 
 The company is aiming to open in  February 2028 , weather permitting, Buc-ee’s founder and CEO Arch “Beaver” Aplin III said at the ceremony, according to reports from Developing Lafayette, Acadiana News First and KTBS. 
 The store, by the numbers 
   Where:  3400 Louisiana Ave., at the northeast corner of Interstate 10 and Louisiana Avenue   Cost:  $82 million   Building:  more than 74,000 square feet   Gas:  120 fuel pumps   Parking:  about 700 spaces   Land:  roughly 42 acres  
 The site belonged to the late Charlie Castille, whose family held it for decades. A longtime family friend, James Alfred, told the crowd Castille had been laughed at for buying the land nearly 60 years ago and always meant for it to help the region, Acadiana News First reported. 
 Boudin next to the brisket 
 Expect the chain’s usual lineup of brisket, beef jerky and Beaver Nuggets. Aplin said the Lafayette store will also carry boudin for local customers. Lafayette Mayor-President Monique Blanco Boulet promised “our own Cajun flair” inside. 
 Jobs 
 Mandi Mitchell, president and CEO of the Lafayette Economic Development Authority, said the project should support more than 300 direct and indirect jobs and produce $257 million in personal income, in today’s dollars, over 25 years, Developing Lafayette reported. Aplin talked up the company’s pay, saying Buc-ee’s aims for jobs people can live on. 
 For Vermilion Parish workers, that is a short commute up U.S. 167. None of the reports from the groundbreaking gave a hiring date. The Times will report it when Buc-ee’s starts taking applications for Lafayette. 
 Why it took so long 
 Lafayette first talked with Buc-ee’s in 2014, and a second try in 2016 also stalled, Mitchell said. LEDA picked the effort back up in 2022, and it took close to three more years of work on zoning, road and utility changes, a special economic development district and an incentive package. 
 “We’ve been kind of fighting and banging our head against this for over a decade,” Aplin said, according to Developing Lafayette. 
 Gov. Jeff Landry, who attended, said he pressed the state Department of Transportation and Development to work with the company on interstate access. “When you look at the amount of jobs it creates, the wages that it pays, it’s in an unbelievable location,” he told Acadiana News First. 
 Crews have already started on the foundation and fuel tanks, Developing Lafayette reported. 
 Louisiana’s second 
 Lafayette is the Texas chain’s second Louisiana store. The first is under construction in Ruston, in north Louisiana.

t: SpaceX Wants Up to 456 Starship Launches a Year From Texas, With Landings in the Gulf. The FAA’s Hearings Are Now Online, and Anyone Can Join
d: The FAA moved all five public meetings on SpaceX’s Texas expansion online and gave the public until Dec. 7 to comment. Boosters and ships could come down in the Gulf of America under the plan. Pecan Island is not part of this review.
b:
SpaceX is asking the federal government to let it fly Starship from South Texas as many as 456 times a year, and to bring its giant boosters and ships down in the Gulf of America, the same water that washes up on Vermilion Parish’s coast. 
 People along the Louisiana coast can now weigh in without driving to Texas. In a notice filed Monday and set to be printed in the Federal Register on Tuesday, the Federal Aviation Administration said every public meeting on the plan will be held online, and it pushed the comment deadline back a week, to  Dec. 7 . 
 What SpaceX is asking for 
 Today SpaceX may launch Starship up to 25 times a year from its Boca Chica site at Starbase, Texas, with up to 50 landings, according to the FAA’s original Oct. 14 notice. The new review covers a two-step increase: 
   Phase 1:  up to 100 launches and 200 landings a year, on any day of the week, day or night.   Phase 2:  up to 456 launches and 912 landings a year, weekdays only, which the FAA describes as a mature program it expects “within several years.”  
 The FAA assumes half of the flights would happen at night, between 10 p.m. and 7 a.m. 
 Where the rockets would come down 
 This is the part with a Gulf angle. Under the plan, the Super Heavy booster would land back at the launch site, make a soft landing in the Gulf of America, or be used up during flight. The Starship upper stage could land back at the site, set down in the Gulf, or splash down or be discarded in the open ocean, the notice says. 
 Rockets would head out on launch headings from northeast to east-southeast, toward the open Gulf. The notice does not say how close to Louisiana any water landing could come. That is exactly the kind of question the scoping period is meant to collect. 
 The FAA says it will study noise, air quality, fish and wildlife, coastal resources, wetlands and water, among other effects, and is consulting with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and the National Marine Fisheries Service on protected species. The only alternative it lists is “No Action,” which would keep SpaceX at today’s limits. 
 How to take part 
 The FAA will hold five identical online meetings. Each opens with a half-hour presentation, then the public may speak for up to three minutes. Registration is required on the  FAA’s project page . 
   Tuesday, Nov. 17:  1-3 p.m. and 5:30-7:30 p.m. Central   Wednesday, Nov. 18:  5:30-7:30 p.m. Central   Thursday, Nov. 19:  1-3 p.m. and 5:30-7:30 p.m. Central  
 Written comments go to  Regulations.gov , docket  FAA-2026-12808 , by Dec. 7. Paper comments go by mail to the address in the notice: “Ms. Amy Hanson, FAA Environmental Protection Specialist, SpaceX Boca Chica, c/o Kimley-Horn, 767 Eustis Street, Suite 100, St. Paul, MN 55114.” The FAA warns that everything sent to the docket is posted online as written, including names and addresses. 
 Earlier plans called for four in-person meetings in Texas and one online. The agency did not give a reason for the switch beyond saying it wants to keep communities informed. 
 What it means here 
 This review is about the Texas site. Pecan Island is not in it, and nothing in the notice changes the timeline for Starbase Louisiana. 
 But it is the clearest look yet at the pace SpaceX has in mind for Starship, and Texas is where the company is testing the cadence it may one day want in Vermilion Parish. It is also the second FAA action on commercial launches in a week. The agency proposed easing several launch safety rules on Nov. 6, with comments due Dec. 9. [Read that story.](/news/faa-loosens-launch-rules-starbase-louisiana/) 
 A draft environmental study, with another round of public comment, will come later, the FAA says. 
  Update, Nov. 12:  The FAA told the Times these meetings cover the Texas site only and that “SpaceX has not submitted an application for the FAA to evaluate proposed Starship operations in Louisiana.” [Read more.](/news/faa-spacex-no-application-starship-louisiana/)
