t: Texas Turned Blue. Here’s What It Could Mean for Starbase Louisiana
d: Democrats won the Texas governor’s race and a U.S. Senate seat after Elon Musk spent heavily against them, and the governor-elect has already asked the state to hold off on a land deal near SpaceX’s Texas launch site. Some industry watchers say that could push SpaceX’s future toward Pecan Island.
b:
Texas, the state SpaceX calls home, voted Democratic up and down the ballot on Tuesday. For Vermilion Parish, the question is whether that makes Starbase Louisiana more important to Elon Musk. 
 What happened in Texas 
 Democrat  Gina Hinojosa  defeated Republican Gov. Greg Abbott, becoming the first Democrat to win the governor’s office in 36 years, Click2Houston and other Texas outlets reported. She takes office Jan. 19, 2027. 
 Democrat  James Talarico , a 37-year-old state legislator and former middle school teacher, beat Republican Ken Paxton for a U.S. Senate seat, the Associated Press reported. He will be Texas’ first Democratic U.S. senator since 1993, and his win ended a 32-year Republican streak in statewide races, according to Houston Public Media. 
 Musk backed the losing side. He spent an estimated $474 million on Republican campaigns in this year’s midterms, nearly half of it in Texas, according to a New York Times estimate cited by Ars Technica. 
 The first move touches SpaceX 
 Two days after the election, at her first news conference as governor-elect, Hinojosa said that morning she had phoned the head of Texas Parks and Wildlife, the state’s park agency, herself. Her request: no action, during the transition, on state land near Boca Chica Beach, next to SpaceX’s Starbase launch site in Cameron County, Click2Houston reported. 
 The agency’s governing commission had a draft agenda that included talk of possibly giving up about 1,300 acres of public land there, according to earlier reporting by the Texas Tribune cited by Click2Houston. The item was dropped from the final agenda. The governor-elect didn’t say if the agency agreed, or what she plans once she takes office. 
 Musk’s first public reaction to the results, posted on X early Wednesday, was one line: “Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now,” Ars Technica reported. 
 Where Louisiana comes in 
 Louisiana stayed Republican. Some industry watchers think that matters for Pecan Island. In an analysis piece, the technology site Ars Technica wrote that the Texas results “may accelerate Musk’s move to Louisiana.” In its view, south Louisiana was headed toward becoming SpaceX’s long-term home for flying hundreds or thousands of Starships a year anyway. The site also said that no one it spoke with expects SpaceX to move its headquarters out of Texas any time soon, though “it’s not impossible” Starbase Louisiana could become headquarters eventually. 
 That is analysis, not a company announcement. SpaceX has said nothing publicly about changing its plans for either state. 
 What the public record does show is that SpaceX is pressing ahead in Louisiana. On Nov. 6, after the election, the company posted two new Pecan Island environmental permitting jobs, bringing its Louisiana openings to nine, according to its job board. One of them, an air-permit engineer, will handle permits in both Texas and Louisiana and can be based at Starbase Louisiana. [Read more about those jobs.](/news/spacex-pecan-island-jobs-wetlands-air-permits/) 
 Starbase Louisiana’s approvals run through Louisiana and federal agencies, not Texas. That includes the parish’s tax agreement, which three residents and a citizens group are challenging in court, along with Army Corps wetland permits and FAA launch licenses. Construction is expected to begin in 2027.

t: Justice Department Awards East Baton Rouge Parish $63.5 Million to Fight Violent Crime
d: Baton Rouge is one of four places picked for the Trump administration’s new Model Cities Initiative, a nearly $300 million federal crime effort. The three-year grant will pay for officers, prosecutors, technology and crime labs.
b:
The federal government is sending  $63,532,285  to East Baton Rouge Parish to fight violent crime, the U.S. Department of Justice announced Thursday. It is one of the largest public safety grants Louisiana’s capital has ever received. 
 The money comes through the department’s  Model Cities Initiative , which it launched in June 2026 to spend nearly $300 million on local crime-fighting plans. Baton Rouge was picked from nearly 50 applicants, the department said, for its partnerships among police, local government and community groups and for its plans to add investigators and prosecutors and modernize crime data. 
 The other places chosen are Jacksonville, Fla.; Jackson, Miss.; and St. Louis. 
 Why Baton Rouge 
 The Justice Department said Baton Rouge’s homicide rate has run about triple the average for big American cities for two decades. From 2021 through 2025, it said, Baton Rouge police answered more than 1,300 shootings in which no one died, more than 12,000 shots-fired calls and more than 1,200 armed robberies. 
 What the money pays for 
 According to the release, the grant can be used to: 
  Hire sworn officers and civilian staff for enforcement, prosecution and related work  Buy or lease equipment and new technology  Expand forensic and crime lab capacity  Pay for mental health and substance use services aimed at keeping people from reoffending  
 The department says it will work with the parish to finalize the plan before the money is spent. 
 What leaders said 
 “This grant is one of the most historic and significant public safety investments in Baton Rouge’s history,” said Sid Edwards, mayor-president of East Baton Rouge Parish, who said the city wants to turn the three-year grant into “a 30-year return on investment.” 
 Gov. Jeff Landry said the award “will help us take more criminals off our streets.” U.S. Sen. Bill Cassidy credited the mayor, the district attorney and others “for entering a winning application,” and Attorney General Liz Murrill said it shows federal and state partners are “fighting back against violent crime.” 
 U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche said the selected cities “are setting an example of proactive law enforcement.” 
 What it means here 
 The money goes only to East Baton Rouge Parish; Vermilion Parish and its law enforcement agencies are not part of this award. The Justice Department said it hopes the four cities will serve as models for other communities.

t: Coeyn Wise, 20, Wins School Board District C Seat, Becoming the Board’s Youngest Member
d: The 2025 Kaplan High graduate beat Harry “Gregg” Meaux 902 to 688 on Election Day. He says his years as a student in the parish’s schools are the best experience he brings.
b:
Vermilion Parish has a School Board member who was sitting in its classrooms not long ago. 
 Coeyn Wise won the  District C  seat on the Vermilion Parish School Board on Nov. 3, defeating Harry “Gregg” Meaux  902 votes to 688 , or 56.7% to 43.3%, with all eight of the district’s precincts counted, according to the Louisiana Secretary of State’s results. Both candidates ran without a party label. 
 Wise is 20, a 2025 graduate of Kaplan High School and now a political science major at LSU, according to his Facebook page. KLFY reported that he is the youngest person ever elected to the board. 
 “A product of the school system” 
 Wise told KLFY that his recent time as a student is the most valuable thing he brings to the board. “I know what works and doesn’t work on the ground,” he said. 
 He said he ran on four priorities: support for teachers, support for special education, transparency, and more career and technical education. 
 Winning, he said, came with “a huge sense of responsibility.” He added that he wants no special treatment because of his age: “I expect to be held to the exact same standard as any other board member.” 
 Wise also said he was encouraged to see other young people win office this year, a sign, in his words, that voters are “willing to give someone in my generation a shot.” 
 The Vermilion Times would like to hear from District C parents, teachers and students: what do you want your new board member to take on first? Tell us in the comments on Facebook.

t: Gueydan Sets Dec. 1 Budget Hearing as Town Moves $195,000 From Utilities to Cover Payroll and Bills
d: Town records also show Gueydan is asking the state again for money to build a new police and fire station, and a state water project ruled ineligible. Both men in the Dec. 12 mayor’s runoff sit on the board that voted on these items.
b:
Gueydan residents will get a chance to weigh in on the town’s money next month. A public hearing on two budgets is set for  Tuesday, Dec. 1, at 5:45 p.m.  at City Hall, according to the agenda the town posted for its November meeting. The council plans to take final votes at its regular meeting right after, at 6 p.m. 
 The hearing covers an  amended budget for 2026  and a  proposed operating budget for 2027 . Both were up for introduction at the board’s Nov. 4 meeting. The town had not posted minutes of that meeting as of Sunday. 
 Utility money covering payroll 
 Gueydan has been shifting money out of its utility fund, which collects water, sewer and gas payments, to cover general expenses. The Board of Aldermen ratified  $120,000  in transfers from the utility fund to the general fund in September, according to the minutes of its Oct. 9 meeting, plus  $7,431.64  from the sales tax fund. The town’s October agenda labels those transfers as going to payroll, bills and BCBS, the Blue Cross Blue Shield health insurance. 
 The November agenda lists another  $75,000  moved from utilities to the general fund during October, again marked for payroll and bills. The board was set to ratify those transfers Nov. 4. 
 Police and fire station, water project 
 Larry Cramer of Sellers & Associates, the town’s engineering firm, advised the board to reapply for state capital outlay money for a new  police and fire station . The minutes say the project was ranked Priority 5 in the last round. The board passed a resolution to apply for the 2027-2028 program and committed the town to pay at least  25%  of the cost, plus any overruns. Mayor Jude Reese is authorized to sign the paperwork. 
 Cramer also told the board the state’s  Louisiana Water Initiative  has ruled a town project ineligible. The firm planned a call with the state to find out why, according to the minutes. 
 Other business 
  The town’s Oct. 6 regular meeting did not happen: no quorum showed up and no one attended, the minutes say. The board met three days later, with Mayor Pro Tem John Laseter presiding and Aldermen Laurel Portie and Anita Dupuis absent.  Two old town Ford pickups were declared junk. A vote to declare the town’s John Deere tractor surplus was put off, and it returned on the November agenda.  Alderman Efrem Livingston asked for an ordinance requiring dog kennels to have a washout connected to the sewer. The board tabled it to get more information, and it is also back on the November agenda.  Town employees get  Christmas Eve  as a paid holiday this year.  
 The runoff connection 
 The two candidates in Gueydan’s Dec. 12 mayor’s runoff,  Jason Suire  and  Efrem “Zim” Livingston , are both aldermen. Suire made or seconded nearly every motion at the Oct. 9 meeting, and Livingston seconded several, including the transfers. The budget hearing falls 11 days before voters choose between them. 
  Gueydan no longer has a newspaper of its own. The Vermilion Times reads the town’s meeting records and covers Gueydan regularly. Want to help? We’re looking for a [Gueydan correspondent](/send-news/#write).

t: SpaceX Posts Two Environmental Permit Jobs for Starbase Louisiana: Wetlands and Air Pollution
d: The new openings show what the company needs before it can build at Pecan Island, Army Corps wetland permits, Louisiana coastal-zone approvals and state air permits, including for on-site power generation. That brings SpaceX’s Pecan Island listings to nine.
b:
SpaceX added two Starbase Louisiana job openings Friday evening, and both are about the permits the company needs before it can build. The listings bring the number of SpaceX openings located in Pecan Island to  nine , according to the company’s public job board, checked by The Vermilion Times on Saturday. 
 Wetlands: Army Corps and coastal-zone permits 
 The first posting,  Sr. Environmental Engineer, Wetlands & Regulatory Compliance , is for someone to manage wetland permits “across multiple sites and Corps Districts.” The job centers on U.S. Army Corps of Engineers permits under Section 404 of the Clean Water Act and Section 10 of the Rivers and Harbors Act, which cover filling wetlands and working in navigable waters. 
 The engineer would also handle Endangered Species Act compliance and environmental reviews under the National Environmental Policy Act, which can range from a short categorical exclusion to a full Environmental Impact Statement. SpaceX says it prefers candidates who know Louisiana’s Joint Permit Application, the state process for projects in the Louisiana Coastal Zone. The person would be the main contact with the Corps, the EPA and state environmental agencies, including on site visits and jurisdictional determinations, the formal rulings on which land counts as regulated wetland. 
 Air permits, including for power plants 
 The second posting,  Sr. Environmental Regulatory Engineer, Air Permitting , would run the company’s air permit work in both states “for power generation and rocket propulsion programs.” The hire could work out of Starbase Louisiana or one of two Texas locations, Starbase or Bastrop. The engineer would deal with the Louisiana Department of Environmental Quality, the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality and the EPA. 
 According to the listing, the power work includes on-site plants that supply “a large, steady electric load” right where they sit, frequently added a phase at a time as demand rises. It lists major-source permits such as Prevention of Significant Deterioration and Title V operating permits. Those permits require emission inventories, pollution-control reviews and air dispersion modeling. The posting covers both states and does not say what will be built at Pecan Island. 
 Neither listing gives a salary. Both ask for a bachelor’s degree and at least five years of experience in the field (seven for the air permit job). 
 Every Pecan Island opening 
 As of Saturday, SpaceX lists these nine jobs at Pecan Island: 
  Sr. Construction Project Manager (Starship Infrastructure, Louisiana)  Civil Engineer, Land Development (Starbase Infrastructure, Louisiana)  Sr. Government Affairs Manager  Sr. Construction Safety Engineer  Sr. Environmental Engineer  Sr. Manager, Environmental Health & Safety  Communications Lead   Sr. Environmental Engineer, Wetlands & Regulatory Compliance  (new Nov. 6)   Sr. Environmental Regulatory Engineer, Air Permitting  (new Nov. 6)  
 See our [running list of every SpaceX Louisiana job](/news/spacex-louisiana-jobs-pecan-island/) and how to apply.

t: FAA Proposes Easing the Launch Safety Rules Starbase Louisiana Would Fly Under; Public Comment Opens Monday
d: Three proposals on file with the Federal Register would change when a rocket must be stopped in flight and how falling debris is judged. The agency also says it wants power to waive some environmental rules and is asking where new spaceports should go.
b:
The federal agency that will decide whether rockets fly from Pecan Island is rewriting the rulebook those rockets would fly under. 
 The Federal Aviation Administration on Thursday announced three proposed changes to its commercial launch safety rules and a final rule of technical fixes. The documents are on file with the Federal Register and are scheduled to be formally published on  Monday, Nov. 9 , according to the Register’s public inspection list. That starts a  30-day public comment period , which would run to about Dec. 9. 
 The rules cover every FAA-licensed commercial launch and reentry in the country. SpaceX’s planned Starbase Louisiana in Vermilion Parish, where construction is expected to start in 2027, would need FAA licenses to fly. The Vermilion Times read all four filings. 
 What the FAA is proposing 
 All three proposals amend Part 450, the set of licensing rules the FAA adopted in 2020. Each says it carries out a 2025 executive order from President Trump that told the Transportation Department to “reevaluate, amend, or rescind” those rules to make licensing faster. 
   When a rocket can keep flying (docket FAA-2026-9943).  Today’s rules let an operator stop arming its “flight abort” system, the system that destroys or shuts down a rocket that strays off course, once certain safety conditions are met. The proposal says that exception applies phase by phase during a flight. The FAA’s release says the change would let operators switch abort capability on and off in flight.   When a rocket must be stopped (docket FAA-2026-9937).  The FAA says launch companies have been confused by the wording on how to set “flight safety limits,” the lines that trigger an abort. It proposes rewriting that paragraph to spell out which inputs count.   Falling debris (docket FAA-2026-9942).  When a spent stage or spacecraft falls back to Earth out of control, operators must show it won’t cause a disaster with many casualties. The proposal adds another way to pass that test: showing the vehicle would break up enough in the atmosphere, payloads included.   Technical corrections.  A final rule fixes six typos and unclear passages and takes effect on publication. The FAA says it changes nothing of substance.  
 Environmental rules and new spaceports 
 In the same announcement, the FAA said it has also issued a proposed rule that would let it waive “unnecessary” environmental laws and regulations it says are slowing space companies down. The release did not identify that proposal by number, and The Vermilion Times could not find it in the Federal Register on Friday. The Times will report its details, and how to comment on it, when it is published. 
 The agency also said it is asking the public and the industry where new spaceports should be built and how to set aside “priority airspace” for launch routes. It said it expects as many as 1,000 launches a year by 2030 and 10,000 licensed launches and reentries a year by 2035, up from 217 U.S. commercial launches in 2025. A full overhaul of the licensing rules is planned for 2027. 
 Transportation Secretary Sean P. Duffy said the changes are about “getting rid of the outdated rules that hold innovators back” while “never compromising on safety.” 
  Update, Nov. 9:  The three proposals were formally published in the Federal Register on Monday (91 FR 70813, 70817 and 70821).  Comments are due Wednesday, Dec. 9, 2026.  
 How to comment 
 Anyone can comment once the proposals are published. Go to regulations.gov and search for the docket number (FAA-2026-9943, FAA-2026-9937 or FAA-2026-9942), or mail comments to Docket Operations, U.S. Department of Transportation, 1200 New Jersey Avenue SE, Washington, DC 20590. Comments are posted publicly, including any personal information you put in them. 
 The FAA is also hiring aerospace engineers for its commercial space office; it says applications are due Dec. 4.

t: Abbeville Meridional and Kaplan Herald Sold to Kentucky-Based Paxton Media Group
d: The parish’s two longtime weeklies are among 14 Acadiana-area papers, plus a printing plant in Eunice, that Louisiana State Newspapers has sold to the family-owned chain from Paducah. The price was not disclosed.
b:
Vermilion Parish’s two oldest newspapers have a new owner. Paxton Media Group, a family-owned chain based in Paducah, Ky., has bought the publishing and printing business of Louisiana State Newspapers, including the  Abbeville Meridional  and the  Kaplan Herald , according to an announcement dated Nov. 2 and posted on the papers’ own website, Vermilion Today. 
 The deal covers 14 community papers across Acadiana and nearby parishes, along with Louisiana State Printing, the company’s press plant in Eunice. That plant prints all 14 papers and more than a dozen titles for other publishers in the region. Neither side disclosed the price. Dirks, Van Essen & April, a newspaper brokerage in Santa Fe, N.M., represented the seller. 
 The papers in the sale 
 Besides the Meridional and the Herald, the sale includes the Eunice News, Church Point News, Ville Platte Gazette, Basile Weekly, Kinder Courier, Oakdale Journal, Morgan City Review, Franklin Banner-Tribune, Bayou Pioneer in Pierre Part, Rayne Acadian-Tribune, Crowley Post-Signal and The Teche News in St. Martin Parish. 
 Who is buying 
 Paxton is a fifth-generation family company founded in 1896 and led today by Jamie Paxton, its president and CEO. The announcement says it publishes more than 120 community newspapers in 15 states and owns WPSD-TV, the NBC station in Paducah. Until now its only Louisiana paper was the Daily Star in Hammond. 
 “We believe local newspapers play an important role in the communities they serve,” Jamie Paxton said in the announcement, adding that the company is “committed to supporting these publications, their employees and their continued success.” The company said the papers will keep covering their towns in print and online. 
 Who is selling 
 Louisiana State Newspapers began in 1963, when Braxton “B.I.” Moody III bought the Rayne Acadian-Tribune and the Church Point News. It incorporated in 1973 and at its peak owned 33 newspapers, making it the largest chain in the state by number of titles, according to the announcement. 
 The announcement does not say whether staffing, print days or subscription prices at the Meridional or the Herald will change. The Vermilion Times will report any changes for local readers as they are announced.

t: Sheriff: Scammers Are Calling Families of People in the Parish Jail, Asking for Money to ‘Release’ Them
d: The callers know the inmate’s name and charge from public arrest records. The Sheriff’s Office says never send money before calling the jail yourself. Separately, deputies are looking for a man seen on video taking batteries and a weed eater from a business on LA 167.
b:
If someone calls saying they can get your relative out of the Vermilion Parish jail for a fee, hang up and call the jail. That’s the warning from Sheriff Eddie Langlinais and Warden Sammy LaPorte of the Vermilion Parish Correctional Center. 
 In a statement released Monday, the Sheriff’s Office said it has had reports of scammers phoning the families of people recently booked into the jail and demanding money in exchange for a promised release. The callers make the pitch believable by using details anyone can find in public arrest records, such as the person’s name and the charges they were booked on. 
 “We have received reports of scammers contacting family members and requesting money under the false promise of securing their loved one’s release from jail,” the statement said. Langlinais and LaPorte urged families “to remain vigilant and never send money without first verifying the legitimacy of the request by contacting VPCC at (337) 898-4430.” 
 How to protect yourself 
   Knowing the charge proves nothing.  Arrest information is public, so a caller who knows it is not necessarily calling from the jail or a court.   Don’t pay a stranger who calls you.  Don’t wire money, buy gift cards or give out bank or card numbers to anyone who contacts you out of the blue about a release.   Call the jail yourself.  Use the number in the Sheriff’s statement above, or the correctional center’s line on the Sheriff’s Office website, (337) 898-4424, which is staffed around the clock.  
 Deputies seek suspect in LA 167 theft 
 In a separate case, the Sheriff’s Office is asking for help identifying a man it says stole from Sunshine Quality Solutions on LA 167. 
 Deputies say surveillance video caught the man carrying off a Stihl string trimmer and several batteries made by John Deere. His car was a blue Dodge Dart, black racing stripe along the side, possibly wearing a fake temporary tag, according to the Sheriff’s Office. No one has been charged. 
 Anyone who recognizes the man or the car is asked to call Detective Sonya Couvillon of the Sheriff’s Criminal Investigations Division at (337) 898-4403. To stay anonymous, call Crime Stoppers of Vermilion at (337) 740-8477, which can pay a cash reward for tips that lead to an arrest.

t: Giant Omelette Weekend: Abbeville’s Celebration Runs Saturday and Sunday, With the Skillet Lit Sunday Afternoon
d: The Confrérie d’Abbeville’s festival fills downtown Nov. 7-8 with music, crafts, an antique car show and a tractor egg-cracking contest. The omelette itself is cooked only on Sunday, starting around 1:30 p.m.
b:
Downtown Abbeville turns into one big breakfast this weekend. The Giant Omelette Celebration runs  Saturday, Nov. 7, and Sunday, Nov. 8 , according to the schedule posted by the Confrérie d’Abbeville, the group that puts on the festival. 
 One thing to know before you go:  the omelette is cooked on Sunday afternoon only.  Saturday is music, food, crafts and old machinery; the big skillet comes out on Sunday. 
 Saturday, Nov. 7 
   9 a.m. to 5 p.m.:  antique implement display (visitors vote for a favorite), arts and crafts show and food show   9 to 10:30 a.m.:  fiddlers and dancers from LeBlanc Elementary, plus Vermilion Parish’s Lache Pas middle school students   10 a.m. to 3 p.m.:  Kids World games and activities   11 a.m. to 1:30 p.m.:  music by Blake Miller & the Old Fashioned Aces   1:30 p.m.:  tractor “egg cracking” contest, adults only, with trophies   2 to 5 p.m.:  Hunter Courville and Cajun Fever   5 p.m.:  grounds close for the night  
 Sunday, Nov. 8 
   6 a.m.:  registration for the “Bikes, Brews & Omelettes Two” bike ride (run through LaTrail.org)   9 a.m.:  official Mass at St. Mary Magdalen Catholic Church   9 a.m. to 4:30 p.m.:  arts and crafts and food shows; antique cars and implements on view until 5 p.m.   10 a.m. to 1 p.m.:  Geno Delafose & French Rockin’ Boogie   1 p.m.:  the chefs and the eggs parade toward the skillet   1:15 p.m.:  the TABASCO Girls Dance Team on Concord Street, and LeBlanc Elementary French immersion students singing   1:30 p.m.:  Fa Tras, a local Cajun band   1:30 to 4:30 p.m.:  the omelette is made and served   4:30 p.m.:  festival ends  
 The procession is the signal that cooking is about to start. Confrérie members in chef’s dress walk through downtown, greeting the crowd, then lead the way down Concord Street to the 12-foot skillet, the festival says. French bread from Poupart’s Bakery in Lafayette travels with the procession and is sliced and served alongside the omelette. 
 The weather 
 It will feel like fall. The National Weather Service in Lake Charles is forecasting a partly sunny Saturday in Abbeville with a high near 74 and a north wind around 10 mph. Saturday night turns mostly cloudy with a low around 47, so bring a jacket for an early start Sunday. Sunday calls for partly sunny skies and a high near 68. 
 If you have questions 
 The Confrérie lists a general information line at 337-344-9232, and contacts for each event are on its website, giantomelette.org. Next year’s celebration is set for Nov. 6-7, 2027.

t: Abbeville Woman, 69, Killed When Car Overturns on LA 86 Near New Iberia
d: She was a passenger and was thrown from the car early Tuesday, State Police said. She is the second Abbeville woman killed in a crash in four days, and troopers say neither was wearing a seat belt.
b:
A 69-year-old woman from Abbeville was killed early Tuesday, Election Day, when the car she was riding in left a curve on LA 86 near New Iberia and rolled over, Louisiana State Police said. 
 Troopers from Troop I were called shortly before 2 a.m. on Nov. 3 to the single-car crash on LA 86 near Dumas Judice Road in Iberia Parish, according to the agency’s news release. 
 What troopers found 
 A 2019 Nissan Sentra was headed east on LA 86 toward Dumas Judice Road when, for reasons still under investigation, it did not make a right-hand curve, ran off the road and overturned, troopers said. 
 Neither person in the car was buckled in, and both were thrown out. The woman, who was the passenger, died at the scene. The driver was taken to a hospital with moderate injuries. 
 Troopers do not suspect impairment, according to the release. As is routine, a toxicology sample was taken and sent for testing. The crash remains under investigation. 
 State Police have not released the names of the woman or the driver. The Vermilion Times does not name crash victims unless their families or officials make the name public. 
 Two Abbeville women in four days 
 It is the second time in four days that an Abbeville woman has died in a crash in a neighboring parish. On Oct. 31, a 28-year-old Abbeville woman was killed near Duson when her car was rear-ended on LA 343; troopers booked the other driver on a vehicular homicide charge. [Our story.](/news/abbeville-woman-killed-duson-crash-dwi-arrest/) State Police said she was not wearing a seat belt either. 
 In Tuesday’s release, the agency urged drivers and passengers to buckle up every trip, saying proper restraint use greatly lowers the risk of serious injury or death. 
 State Police Troop I public affairs can be reached at 337-262-5880.

t: Vermilion Parish Election Results: Landry Wins DA Race, Broussard Wins Erath Mayor, Gueydan Heads to Runoff
d: Unofficial final returns: Don Landry is the 15th Judicial District’s next district attorney, Stephanie Broussard will lead Erath, and Gueydan picks its mayor in a Dec. 12 runoff. Both parish tax renewals passed.
b:
Updated 5:50 a.m. Wednesday.  All precincts have reported statewide, in Vermilion Parish and across the 15th Judicial District, according to unofficial returns from the Louisiana Secretary of State. The results become official once the state certifies them. 
 Landry wins district attorney 
 Donald “Don” Landry defeated Kristian Earles to become district attorney for the 15th Judicial District, which covers Lafayette, Acadia and Vermilion parishes. With all 244 precincts counted, Landry had 60,606 votes (55.9%) to Earles’ 47,878 (44.1%). Vermilion voters gave Landry an even bigger edge, 10,513 to 6,058, or 63.4%. 
 Local winners (unofficial) 
   Mayor of Erath:  Stephanie P. Broussard beat Marlene Menard, 561 to 221 (71.7%).   Erath police chief:  Randall Toups beat Anna Lapointe, 418 to 370.   Maurice police chief:  John Dayries beat Guy Nerren, 553 to 447, after the two were tied in early voting.   Abbeville City Council, District A:  William “Billy” Noegel beat Cornelius Darby, 465 to 252.   Kaplan city marshal:  William J. Seaux beat Ruby Thibeaux, 1,641 to 1,264.   School Board District C:  Coeyn Wise beat Harry “Gregg” Meaux, 902 to 688.   School Board District F:  Roderick Darby beat Tyrone Alexander, 820 to 496.   Justice of the Peace, Ward 4:  Cheryl Granger beat Philip DeBaillon, 1,829 to 832.  
 Gueydan mayor: runoff Dec. 12 
 No candidate got a majority. Jason Suire led with 133 votes (36%), Efrem “Zim” Livingston had 121 (32.8%) and Jeffrey Lamson 115 (31.2%), a spread of 18 votes from first to third. Suire and Livingston are set to meet in the Dec. 12 general election on the state’s calendar. 
 Maurice aldermen 
 Six candidates ran for five seats: Troy Catalon (774), Scott Trahan (725), Megan Landry-Lalande (682), Matthew Trahan (643), Wayne Theriot (541) and Jonathan Schlicher (487). Multi-seat races use their own majority rules, and The Vermilion Times will report which seats are settled once the count is certified. 
 Taxes 
 Voters renewed both property taxes on the ballot. Consolidated Gravity Drainage District No. 1’s 16-mill tax passed 2,017 to 1,243 (62%), and Hospital Service District No. 3’s 8.29-mill tax passed 559 to 283 (66%). Both run 10 more years. 
 Congress and Senate 
   U.S. House, 3rd District:  Clay Higgins won another term outright with 55% districtwide, all 571 precincts reporting, avoiding a runoff. He took 69.8% in Vermilion.   U.S. Senate:  Julia Letlow won the seat, beating “Jamie” Davis 745,963 to 720,106 (50.9% to 49.1%) statewide with all 3,722 precincts counted. Her margin narrowed as the last precincts came in overnight. Vermilion went 72% for Letlow.  
 Turnout 
 About 17,400 Vermilion voters cast a ballot in the Senate race, roughly 46% of the parish’s 38,099 registered voters. More than 4,600 of them voted early or absentee. 
 The amendments 
 Vermilion voters approved Amendments 1, 3, 4, 6, 7, 8 and 9 and rejected 2, 5 and 10, matching the final statewide count: Amendments 2, 5 and 10 failed statewide and the other seven passed. Amendment 10, on tax breaks for fixed-up blighted property, lost in Vermilion by just 96 votes.

t: Abbeville Woman, 28, Killed in Halloween Crash Near Duson; Rayne Driver Booked on Vehicular Homicide
d: State Police say a Buick failed to slow on LA 343 and hit the back of her car as she stopped for a stop sign. The other driver’s breath test came back over the legal limit, troopers said.
b:
A 28-year-old woman from Abbeville died early Halloween morning when another car slammed into the back of hers on a rural highway near Duson, and the driver who hit her is jailed on a vehicular homicide charge, according to Louisiana State Police. 
 Troopers from Troop I were called just after midnight on Saturday, Oct. 31, to a two-vehicle wreck on LA 343 at Ridge Road in Lafayette Parish, the agency said in a news release. 
 What troopers say happened 
 The Abbeville woman was driving a 2014 Kia Optima south on LA 343 and slowing down for the stop sign at Ridge Road, according to the State Police. A 2011 Buick LaCrosse was headed the same direction behind her. Troopers say the Buick never slowed and rear-ended the Kia. They have not said why. 
 The woman was not wearing a seat belt, according to the release. She died at the scene. As is routine in fatal crashes, troopers took a toxicology sample from her for testing. 
 State Police have not released her name. The Vermilion Times does not name crash victims unless their families or officials make the name public. 
 The arrest 
 The Buick’s driver, Shawnta Davis-Ned, 40, of Rayne, was not hurt. She was also unbuckled, troopers said. A breath test showed her blood alcohol concentration was over the legal limit, according to the State Police, which did not give the number. 
 Davis-Ned was booked into the Lafayette Parish Correctional Center on charges of: 
  Vehicular homicide  First-offense driving while impaired  Careless operation  Not wearing a seat belt  
 An arrest is an accusation, not a conviction. The crash remains under investigation. 
 A reminder from troopers 
 The State Police used the release to urge drivers to plan a sober ride. Alcohol, prescription drugs and other drugs slow reaction time and dull the vision and coordination a driver needs, the agency said. Its message: “if you feel different, you drive different.” 
 The State Police’s Troop I public affairs office can be reached at 337-262-5880.

t: SpaceX Posts a Ninth Starbase Louisiana Job: A Second Communications Lead for Pecan Island
d: The new opening, posted Monday on SpaceX’s job board, is a second community-outreach role for the site. Like the first, it must work at Pecan Island full time.
b:
SpaceX now has nine job openings listed for its planned Starbase Louisiana site, up from eight at the end of last week, according to the company’s public job board, which The Vermilion Times checks every day. 
 The new listing, titled simply “Communications Lead,” went up Monday at 12:13 p.m. It is the second communications job for the site. The first, “Communications Lead – Pecan Island,” was posted Oct. 12 and is still open. 
 What the job is 
 The two postings carry the same description. The person hired would handle outreach with the communities around the site, give hands-on public relations support at events, keep up relationships with local partners, and coach SpaceX executives for speaking engagements and public appearances. The job also includes building communication plans for “crisis situations.” 
 One line in both listings stands out: the role is to develop strategies “that get the public excited about how artificial intelligence will help and support SpaceX and its affiliates’ positions as a positive impact in the community.” The posting does not explain what part artificial intelligence would play at the Louisiana site. 
 Requirements 
  A bachelor’s degree and at least five years of experience in communications, events or content development  Strong writing and social media skills  Willingness to work extended hours and weekends  Full-time work on site at Pecan Island; hybrid and remote work will not be considered  U.S. citizenship, permanent residency or another status allowed under federal export rules (ITAR)  
 The listing does not give a salary. 
  Update, Nov. 4:  The Principal Construction Project Engineer listing has since been removed from SpaceX’s board, so eight Pecan Island openings remain. 
 The nine openings 
 The board now lists two communications leads, a government affairs manager, two construction project leaders, a civil engineer, a construction safety engineer, an environmental engineer and an environmental health and safety manager, all at Pecan Island. [See the full list from last week.](/news/spacex-louisiana-jobs-pecan-island/) The live count is always on our [Starbase Watch page](/starbase/#lv-jobs-h). 
 Have a question for SpaceX about the Louisiana site? [Send it to the Times](/send-news/) and we will put it to the company.

t: Vote Early in the Day Tuesday: Storms Likely to Build by Afternoon and Evening in Vermilion Parish
d: The National Weather Service gives Abbeville a 50% chance of rain Tuesday, rising to 60% Tuesday night, with gusts up to 25 mph. Polls are open 6 a.m. to 8 p.m.
b:

t: Nine Killed as Business Jet From Austin Crashes Into Palm Beach County Neighborhood
d: Updated Monday: The NTSB says there is evidence the Learjet began breaking up before it hit the ground, minutes after the crew reported ice and turbulence at 35,000 feet.
b:
Update, Monday: what the NTSB said 
 Tom Chapman, a member of the National Transportation Safety Board, told reporters in West Palm Beach on Monday that investigators have “some evidence that there was some breakup of the aircraft before impact,” as reported by WPEC and The Associated Press. He said parts of the jet may turn up some distance from where it hit. 
 Chapman laid out the final minutes, based on the crew’s radio calls, according to WPEC: 
  The jet left Austin around 10:37 a.m. with two crew members and seven passengers.  About 12:47 p.m., cruising at 35,000 feet, the pilots radioed that they were picking up a light coating of clear ice, riding through moderate turbulence and drifting about 700 feet off their altitude in air that was 47 below zero Celsius. They said the ice was under control.  The crew then reported precipitation and asked to climb to 37,000 feet, which controllers approved.  About 12:48 p.m., the jet radioed that it was in an “overspeed condition descending.” The rest of the transmission could not be understood.  
 Chapman said the board is looking at whether weather played a role but would not speculate on a cause this early, WPEC reported. Investigator Timothy Monville put the wreckage area at about 2,600 feet long and about 2,100 feet wide, spread over ball fields, businesses and homes. 
 Monville also said a man driving out of the area suffered a leg injury, the first report of anyone hurt on the ground. County Commissioner Joel Flores said about 77 mobile homes were evacuated and gave no timeline for residents to return, according to the AP. 
 Authorities have not yet identified the nine victims publicly. The NTSB asks witnesses to email witness@ntsb.gov and asks anyone who finds debris to leave it where it is. 
 The first hours 
 A business jet carrying nine people slammed into a Palm Beach County, Fla., neighborhood Sunday, killing everyone on board, U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said. 
 “All 9 people on board were killed,” Duffy wrote in a post on X. 
 The plane, a Learjet 60, went down around 12:50 p.m. local time near Cresthaven, according to a statement from the Federal Aviation Administration. The jet left Austin-Bergstrom International Airport headed for North Eleuthera, an island airport in the Bahamas. The FAA said the information is preliminary. 
 On the ground 
 The jet came down along Military Trail near Greenacres, leaving a crater in the road, Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis said after visiting the scene. “Obviously, this was a cataclysmic plane crash,” DeSantis said. 
 Palm Beach County officials said that as of their news conference they had no reports of anyone on the ground being killed or hurt. They said about 600 people living in a nearby mobile home community were expected to be moved out while investigators work, with two shelters ready and county buses on standby, WPTV reported. 
 The county closed Military Trail from 10th Avenue North up to Purdy Lane and Alameda Drive until further notice. 
 The investigation 
 The National Transportation Safety Board is leading the investigation, with the FAA’s help. NTSB investigators were arriving at the site Sunday and Monday morning, and the board scheduled a Monday news conference in West Palm Beach, according to the NTSB. 
 Officials have not said what caused the crash or released the names of the people on board. Recordings and accounts of the pilot’s final radio calls are circulating online; The Vermilion Times has not verified them and will rely on the NTSB’s findings. 
 The FAA usually posts a preliminary report the next business day. The NTSB’s preliminary report typically follows within weeks, and a final cause can take a year or more.

t: Vermilion Parish Early Vote Already Tops 2022 Midterm: 4,658 Ballots Cast Before Tuesday
d: State records show early in-person voting up about 20% over the last midterm. Polls open at 6 a.m. Tuesday and close at 8 p.m.; bring a photo ID.
b:
Vermilion Parish voters have already cast more ballots ahead of Tuesday’s election than they did in the entire early and absentee period of the last midterm, according to a Times review of Secretary of State records. 
 The state’s parish-by-parish report, released Sunday, counts  4,658  early and absentee ballots in Vermilion through Oct. 31. The final count for the November 2022 midterm was  4,255 , a figure that included absentee ballots received up to a week after that election. This year’s total is already about 9% higher, and mail ballots can still arrive. 
 Who has voted 
   Early, in person:  3,726 this year vs. 3,118 in 2022   Absentee or by mail:  932 so far vs. 1,137 in 2022   Total:  4,658 so far vs. 4,255 in 2022  
 In-person early voting is up about 20%. Absentee ballots are behind 2022’s final number so far. 
 By party, Republicans cast 2,581 of the early ballots, about 55%. Democrats cast 1,308, about 28%, and voters with no party or another party cast 769. In 2022, Republicans cast 2,202 early ballots and Democrats 1,382. 
 Women outvoted men, 2,540 to 2,117. White voters cast 3,933 ballots, Black voters 616 and voters of other races 109. 
 How to vote Tuesday 
   Polls open at 6 a.m. and close at 8 p.m.  Anyone in line at 8 p.m. can still vote, according to the Secretary of State.   Bring a photo ID  with your name and signature, such as a driver’s license, a Louisiana special ID, the LA Wallet digital license or a U.S. military ID. Voters without one can fill out a voter identification affidavit.  Find your polling place and sample ballot through the Secretary of State’s Voter Portal or the free GeauxVote app.  Campaigning is not allowed within 600 feet of a polling place.  
 What’s on the ballot 
 Contested races for district attorney, the mayors of Erath and Gueydan, two School Board seats and more, plus 10 statewide constitutional amendments. [See the full ballot.](/news/whats-on-the-ballot-vermilion-parish/) 
 The Vermilion Times will post Vermilion Parish results from the Secretary of State’s count as they come in Tuesday night.

t: Police Jury Approves RV Ordinance, Raises Ordinance Fines to $1,500 and Seeks a Vermilion Levee District
d: Draft minutes of the Oct. 21 meeting, posted on the parish website, show every vote was unanimous. A Gueydan drainage tax renewal is also headed to voters in April.
b:
The Vermilion Parish Police Jury signed off on a parish RV ordinance, voted to raise the fine for breaking parish ordinances to $1,500, and agreed to pursue a new levee district for Vermilion at its Oct. 21 meeting, according to minutes the parish posted online. 
 The minutes are marked “not signed,” meaning they are a draft until jurors approve them at their next regular meeting. Twelve of the 14 jurors attended; Dane Hebert and Mark Poche were absent. Every motion recorded passed unanimously. 
 The RV ordinance 
 Jurors told the parish’s lawyer, Paul Moresi III, to strike every mention of temporary housing other than RVs from the RV ordinance, and voted that once that correction is made, the ordinance is approved. In a second vote they told him to update the code terms supplied by the parish permit specialist. 
 Before that vote, jurors let Vanessa Duhon speak, and she presented information on park model homes, according to the minutes. 
 The minutes do not include the ordinance’s text, and the corrected version had not been posted on the parish website as of Sunday morning. The Vermilion Times will report what the ordinance requires once the final text is public. 
 Fines go to $1,500 
 On a recommendation from the Courthouse/General Needs Committee, jurors approved raising fines for parish ordinance violations to $1,500. The minutes do not say what the fine was before or which ordinances it covers. 
 A levee district of Vermilion’s own 
 Jurors also adopted their coastal committee’s recommendation to create an independent levee district for Vermilion Parish through the Legislature, with the parish’s legal counsel reaching out to Iberia Parish. Going through the Legislature means the idea would need a bill in Baton Rouge. 
 The same vote supports placing a coastal restoration project along the north shore of Vermilion Bay in an area not already funded for rock, and lets the parish advertise for bids on Phase IIA of the North Vermilion Bay Shoreline Protection Project once permits are in hand and the state coastal authority agrees. 
 Gueydan drainage tax heads to the April ballot 
 Jurors approved Resolution 2026-R-24, which lets Sub-District No. 5 of the Gueydan Drainage District hold an election on  Saturday, April 17, 2027 . Voters there will decide whether to renew a 14.04-mill property tax for drainage work for 10 years, 2029 through 2038. The resolution estimates the tax brings in about $284,000 a year. 
 Where else the money went 
   Opioid settlement work:  $33,429.24 to JEPCO Holdings LLC for recovery housing support services for eligible Vermilion residents, paid as part of the parish’s opioid abatement effort.   Courthouse:  $32,858.10 to Minvielle Lumber Company and $1,679.95 to The Sellers Group for third-floor courtroom renovations, and $69,144.30 in two payments to Tilden A. Bonin Contractor for waterproofing and painting the outside of the Courthouse Annex.   Ethics case:  $1,902.50 to the law firm Sternberg, Naccari & White in a state Board of Ethics matter, Docket No. 2023-940.   Juvenile housing:  jurors approved an increase in what the parish pays for juvenile housing. The minutes give no amount.  
 Roads and neighborhoods 
  The parish administrator will ask the state Transportation Department to review the intersection of LA 335 and LA 14.  Pumping Plant Road will get “No Truck Route” signs and lights like the City of Abbeville’s.  Jurors sent blighted-property letters about homes on Lynnedale Loop and Nicole Drive in Abbeville, and approved a preliminary plat for the Stillwater Development on LA 699.  They asked the St. Mary Community Center to add two board members representing the Kaplan, Gueydan, Delcambre and Erath areas.  
 The jury’s committees meet next on Wednesday, Nov. 4. [What’s on those agendas.](/news/police-jury-committees-nov-4-spacex/)

t: Old Paint, Oil and Batteries: Parish Sets Household Hazardous Waste Day for Dec. 12
d: Vermilion Parish residents can drop off chemicals, tires and recyclables for free at the parish solid waste plant, 8 a.m. to 1 p.m. Bring proof you live in the parish.
b:
If there are half-empty paint cans, old motor oil or dead batteries in your shed, the Police Jury has a day for them. 
 The parish will hold a Household Hazardous Waste Collection Day on  Saturday, Dec. 12, from 8 a.m. to 1 p.m.  at the Vermilion Parish Solid Waste Plant, according to a flyer the Police Jury posted. You must bring identification showing you live in Vermilion Parish. Businesses cannot drop off commercial waste. 
 What you can bring 
  Motor oil, antifreeze, transmission fluid and other car maintenance products  Latex and oil-based paints, stains, thinners and solvents  Aerosol cans  Household cleaners, including acids, bleach, furniture polish and wax  Weed killers, bug sprays and other pesticides  Household and car batteries  Tires, off the rim only  Recyclables: aluminum, tin and steel cans; newspapers, magazines, junk mail and cardboard; and plastics marked No. 1 or No. 2  
 What to leave at home 
 Unlabeled containers, anything leaking, medicines and medical waste, ammunition, flares, fireworks or explosives, smoke detectors, gas or propane cylinders, and building junk such as sinks, floor tile, siding and old appliances. Parish workers can turn away anything they consider unsafe. 
 How to get there 
 From U.S. 167, turn west on LA 696 and go about three-quarters of a mile, then turn north on Birch Road and follow it to the end. Parish workers will direct you from there. 
 Questions go to the Vermilion Parish Solid Waste Plant at 337-898-4338.

t: Council on Aging to Ask Police Jury for SpaceX-Related Money; Jurors Set Closed-Door Talk on Starbase Lawsuit
d: The Vermilion Parish Police Jury’s committees meet Wednesday, the day after the election. Here is everything on the agendas, taken from the parish’s own posted documents, and how to speak at the meeting.
b:
The Vermilion Council on Aging plans to ask the Police Jury for money tied to SpaceX on Wednesday, and jurors expect to go behind closed doors to talk about the lawsuit that seeks to undo the parish’s Starbase Louisiana tax deal, according to committee agendas the parish posted this week. 
 The Vermilion Times read every page of the agenda packet. Nothing below comes from another news outlet. 
 When and where 
 The committees meet  Wednesday, Nov. 4 , on the second floor of the Courthouse Building, 100 N. State St., Abbeville, in the Police Jury meeting room. The Coastal Protection & Restoration Committee starts at  4 p.m.  The 911, Courthouse/General Needs, Public Works, Finance and Public Road committees follow, according to a notice from Parish Administrator Keith Roy dated Oct. 30. 
 Each committee agenda opens with a period for public comment on any item it will consider. That is your chance to speak. 
 SpaceX on the agenda 
  Council on Aging request.  Clare Martin of the Vermilion Council on Aging is listed on the Courthouse/General Needs agenda with a “Request for SpaceX Related Funding.” The agenda does not say how much she will ask for or what the money would pay for. 
  The lawsuit, in private.  Under legal counsel, the same committee lists an executive session to discuss  Vermilion Citizens Coalition Inc., Dr. Robert J. Young III, Rebecca C. Young and Cheryl Choate v. Industrial Development Board of the Parish of Vermilion, Louisiana Inc. and Vermilion Parish Police Jury . That is the open-meetings suit asking a court to void the SpaceX tax agreement. Executive sessions are closed to the public, but any vote must be taken in open session. 
 Also on the agendas 
   Coastal committee:  Mike Pugh of Royal Engineering has time on the agenda, along with reports from the parish engineer, the parish’s coastal advocate and the parish administrator. At its Oct. 21 meeting, the jury’s agenda carried a coastal committee recommendation to ask Royal Engineering to attend committee meetings.   Courthouse/General Needs:  presentations from Brandon Trahan, CEO of LaMay Group; Chris Canty of Waterfleet; Pastor August of Nehemiah Projects; and the firm Hunt, Guillot & Associates, which will pitch consulting services. Lloyd Campisi will present the parish’s insurance renewal, and Ebony Cooksey Thomas of Nextlink Internet will give an update on the Gumbo 2.0 broadband program.   Public Works:  reports from Landfill Superintendent and Mosquito Control Director Billy Noegel, Public Works Director Gary Guidry, and John Sonnier, the coyote and USDA beaver specialist. Jurors also list an executive session on possible litigation, after a written demand, against Great Midwest Insurance Company over the Chenier Au Tigre Gap Closure Project.   Finance and Public Road:  reports from the parish administrator, the parish engineer, legal counsel and the road supervisor.  
 Committee recommendations go to the full Police Jury for a final vote at a later regular meeting. 
 Still in effect: the burn ban 
 The parish-wide burn ban that began Oct. 15 remains in force until the Police Jury lifts it by a new proclamation, according to the parish’s posted notice. It bars open burning of brush, yard waste and similar debris, with limited exceptions such as permitted agricultural burning. 
 The Vermilion Times will report what the committees decide.

t: School Board Orders Appraisal of 4,000 Acres Next to Starbase Louisiana Ahead of SpaceX Talks
d: The land near White Lake brings Vermilion Parish schools $20,000 to $30,000 a year in hunting leases. Superintendent Tommy Byler hopes a deal with SpaceX could mean better pay for teachers.
b:
The Vermilion Parish School Board wants to know what its marsh is worth now that SpaceX owns the land around it. 
 Board members voted last week to have roughly 4,000 acres of school-owned land appraised, The Advocate reported. The property sits in the marsh near White Lake, north of Pecan Island, and borders the roughly 125,000 acres SpaceX has gathered for its planned Starbase Louisiana launch site, according to Superintendent Tommy Byler. 
 “How do you appraise marsh land that has a $100 billion industry next to it?” Byler asked, in comments to the newspaper. 
 What the land earns today 
 Right now the acreage pays the school system modestly. Hunting leases bring in about $20,000 to $30,000 a year. 
 Oil and gas once paid far more. Mineral income from school lands topped $6 million in 2014 but fell to about $150,000 in the 2024-25 fiscal year, The Advocate reported. Because that money swings with the market, board policy keeps it out of the general fund that pays for day-to-day operations. 
 Byler said the parcels would not work as future school sites. “Where it’s located is more advantageous for SpaceX to have it than for me to have it,” he said. 
 How a deal could work 
 The acreage is Section 16 land, set aside so it can host a school or earn money for public education. Louisiana law does not let a school board sell it without approval from the Legislature, but a board can sign some leases on its own or trade the land for property of equal value. 
 Byler said the appraisal will take several weeks. Once the figure is in, the board plans to talk among its own members first and then pass the number to SpaceX to open negotiations. He said nobody has discussed yet which properties might be part of a trade, and any final terms would need a vote of the board. 
 The aim, the superintendent said, is to raise revenue for parish schools. He said that could mean “better pay for our teachers.” 
 Another school property in the picture 
 SpaceX already rents the old Pecan Island School site for $1 a year. That property belongs to University of Louisiana at Lafayette Ragin’ Cajun Facilities Inc., according to The Advocate. 
 The Vermilion Times will report the appraisal figure and any School Board vote on a trade or lease when they come.

t: Iran Vows Retaliation ‘Without Geographic Limits’ as Trump Weighs New Strikes After Midterms
d: No new U.S. strike had been announced as of Saturday afternoon. Mediators are working in Qatar to restart talks, and Secretary of State Marco Rubio says the president has not decided.
b:
Iran’s supreme leader told his military on Saturday to answer any new American or Israeli attack right away and to hit back wherever it chooses, while diplomats raced in Qatar to keep the war from restarting after Tuesday’s U.S. midterm elections. 
 As of Saturday afternoon, the United States had not announced any new strike on Iran. Video clips of an earlier presidential address about Iran strikes have been circulating on social media this weekend; they are not from today. 
 What Iran said 
 A statement posted Saturday on the Telegram account of Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei said “any level or type of threat must be met with an immediate, impactful, and geographically unrestricted response,” CNBC reported. Iranian state media said Khamenei met with the country’s top commanders, the first such meeting reported publicly since the war began, and told them to widen their list of possible U.S. and Israeli targets, according to The National News Desk. 
 Khamenei became supreme leader after the Feb. 28 U.S.-Israeli strikes that opened the war killed his father, Ali Khamenei. The younger Khamenei has made no public appearance since then. 
 Iran’s armed forces chief of staff, Maj. Gen. Ali Abdollahi, said any attack would be met with “immense force,” Al Jazeera reported. 
 What Washington said 
 Rubio told reporters the president has not yet decided whether to resume military action, according to Al Jazeera, and said he did not know whether the talks in Qatar have a deadline. 
 According to MS NOW, which cited three officials in the region, the administration has told Gulf partners that American strikes could come as soon as Nov. 4, the day after the election. The White House declined to comment on that report, The National News Desk said. 
 Speaking Tuesday, Trump said the war will end “whenever I want it to,” CNBC reported. 
 The talks in Qatar 
 Qatari mediators spent more than 12 hours in Tehran on Friday trying to restart direct talks between the two countries, a source familiar with the discussions told CNBC. An Iranian delegation went to Doha on Saturday. 
 Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi told Al Jazeera that the U.S. outreach, including a letter from Vice President JD Vance, was “a positive step.” He also said, “We see no need to meet with the Americans at this stage,” and called reports of upcoming meetings “merely media speculation.” 
 One proposal on the table would reopen the Strait of Hormuz within two days. Iran’s conditions include lifting sanctions, fewer U.S. forces in the region, restored oil waivers and the release of frozen funds, among them $6 billion held in Qatar, according to Al Jazeera. 
 Ships, mines and oil 
 Tension on the water is still high. On Saturday an official in Iran’s Hormozgan province said U.S. forces had attacked two fishing boats near Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz, according to Iranian state broadcasting. That claim has not been independently confirmed, and U.S. Central Command did not immediately respond to CNBC. On Friday, Iran said four tankers had hit mines in the strait. 
 Oil has climbed on the uncertainty. Brent crude for December delivery settled Friday at $117.64 a barrel, its highest close since late April, CNBC reported. In a parish where many families work in oil and gas, or simply fill up a truck every few days, that number is felt at home. 
 How we got here 
 The war began Feb. 28 with U.S. and Israeli strikes on Iran. A preliminary deal signed June 17 to stop the fighting fell apart within weeks, and the last confirmed U.S. strikes on Iran were on Sept. 1, according to CNBC. 
 The Vermilion Times will update this story if the United States or Iran announces military action.

t: Who Pays for LA 82? State Hires Landry Donor’s Firm for SpaceX Louisiana Road Work
d: The engineering firm DOTD chose for work around Starbase Louisiana has given $115,000 to a Landry-aligned PAC. The state still won’t say if the job was bid, what it costs, or who covers the road bill.
b:
The state has started lining up engineers for the roads SpaceX will need in southern Vermilion Parish, and the first firm publicly tied to that work is a longtime political donor to Gov. Jeff Landry. 
 Royal Engineers & Consultants, based in New Orleans, is DOTD’s pick to handle work connected to the Starbase Louisiana site near Pecan Island, The Center Square reported Saturday. Campaign records reviewed by the outlet show the firm gave $115,000 over six donations since 2019 to Cajun PAC II, a committee Landry once chaired. The biggest single check, $50,000, came in June 2024. 
 What parish drivers should watch 
 For people who use LA 82, the bigger question is the bill. State agencies are studying routes, bridges and traffic around the launch site, and LA 82 is being looked at for possible improvements, according to the report. Nobody has decided how much of that SpaceX pays and how much falls to taxpayers. 
 What is still unknown 
   Was it bid?  DOTD did not say, according to The Center Square.   What does it cost?  Not disclosed.   What will Royal do?  Not disclosed. The contract runs through 2031.  
 DOTD defended the pick, saying the firm’s Louisiana staff are “strategically located near the SpaceX site.” Royal declined to comment, and the governor’s office had not responded, the outlet reported. 
 Who Royal is 
 The firm is no stranger to state work. It holds more than $44 million in active state contracts and has inspected highway and bridge projects across south Louisiana for two decades, according to the report. Its political giving has crossed party lines, reaching Republicans and Democrats alike over the years. 
 The Times is tracking the road question, and every other piece of the SpaceX project, on  Starbase Watch .

t: Where Is Starbase Louisiana? SpaceX’s Pecan Island Site, Explained
d: SpaceX’s planned launch site covers about 125,000 acres near Pecan Island in southern Vermilion Parish, roughly 27 miles from Kaplan and 30 from Abbeville as the crow flies.
b:
SpaceX is planning Starbase Louisiana on a tract of roughly 125,000 acres in the Pecan Island area of Vermilion Parish, The Center Square reported. SpaceX’s own job postings for the project list their location as Pecan Island, La. 
 [[map]] 
 How far is it? 
 Pecan Island is a small community in the marsh country of southern Vermilion Parish, near the Gulf. Measured in a straight line from the Pecan Island community, using OpenStreetMap’s coordinates: 
   Kaplan:  about 27 miles   Abbeville:  about 30 miles   White Lake:  about 7 miles  
 Driving distances are longer, since roads in the marsh do not run straight. The Times has not seen a published map of the site’s exact boundaries, so these distances are measured to the Pecan Island community, not to a launch pad. 
 What is next to it 
 The Vermilion Parish School District owns six parcels, about 4,000 acres, beside the planned spaceport, on the north side of LA 82 by White Lake, Acadiana News First reported Oct. 28. The land is Section 16 school property, which cannot be sold without legislative approval but can be swapped; it would be appraised before any negotiations. 
 When it will be built 
 Building is slated to start in 2027, with the first launch aimed for 2029, according to The Center Square. SpaceX has begun posting jobs for the site;  the Times lists every opening here . 
 For the full timeline, the money and the open questions, see  Starbase Watch .

t: SpaceX Louisiana Jobs: The First 8 Openings Posted for Pecan Island
d: SpaceX’s own job board lists eight positions at its planned Starbase Louisiana site, all senior engineering, construction, safety and community roles. Here is every one.
b:
SpaceX has started hiring for Starbase Louisiana. As of Saturday, the company’s public job board lists eight openings located in Pecan Island, La., the first jobs tied to the planned launch site in Vermilion Parish, according to a review of the listings by The Vermilion Times. 
 All eight are senior professional roles focused on getting the site built: civil and construction engineering, construction management, safety, environmental compliance, government affairs and communications. None lists a salary. 
 Every SpaceX opening at Pecan Island 
 Listed with the date each was first posted: 
   Sr. Construction Project Manager  (Starship Infrastructure, Louisiana), Sept. 16   Civil Engineer, Land Development  (Starbase Infrastructure, Louisiana), Sept. 17   Sr. Government Affairs Manager , Oct. 6   Communications Lead, Pecan Island , Oct. 12   Sr. Construction Safety Engineer , Oct. 15   Sr. Environmental Engineer , Oct. 15   Sr. Manager, Environmental Health & Safety , Oct. 15   Principal Construction Project Engineer  (Starship Infrastructure, Louisiana), Oct. 23  
 The government affairs posting says the role will work with “internal and external stakeholders” to help ensure SpaceX has “a robust and continually growing relationship with the local community.” The environmental, health and safety manager will oversee programs “at the Starship high-rate launch site,” the listing says. 
 For comparison, the same job board lists about 450 openings at SpaceX’s existing Starbase site in Texas. 
 How many jobs are coming 
 SpaceX’s Louisiana site is supposed to grow to 3,000 direct jobs within ten years, paying $92,600 a year on average, according to The Center Square. Building is slated to start in 2027 and launches in 2029. 
 Whether those jobs go to Vermilion Parish residents is an open question. The parish’s tax deal with SpaceX treats hiring locals as a goal, not a rule, according to the citizens’ group Vermilion United, as reported by Acadiana News First.
