t: Starbase Louisiana: What Vermilion Parish Knows So Far
d: The jobs, the money, the timeline and the questions still open about SpaceX’s planned launch site near Pecan Island, in one place.
b:
Most of what Vermilion Parish has learned about Starbase Louisiana has arrived in pieces, from a ribbon-cutting announcement to lawsuits and records requests. Here it is in one place, with where each piece came from. 
 What is SpaceX building? 
 A launch site for Starship on a tract of roughly 125,000 acres in the Pecan Island area, which the company bills as the world’s largest spaceport, according to The Center Square. SpaceX’s own job postings for the project list Pecan Island as the location.  Here is where that is.  
 When? 
 Groundbreaking is penciled in for 2027 and the first launch for 2029, per The Center Square. 
 How many jobs? 
 The outlet reports a target of 3,000 direct jobs within ten years, at an average of $92,600 a year. SpaceX has already posted its first eight openings for the site.  See them all.  Whether the jobs go to locals is not guaranteed: the parish tax agreement treats local hiring as a goal, not a rule, Acadiana News First reported. 
 What does the parish get, and give up? 
 SpaceX’s yearly payments to the parish open at $25 million and climb 2% a year for 25 years, about $800 million altogether by the Gulf States Newsroom’s math, as reported by WWNO. On the other side of the ledger, the newsroom pegs the property tax break near $23.8 billion over those years. The Center Square values the whole state-and-local incentive package around $27.5 billion. 
 How was it approved? 
 The parish Industrial Development Board signed off Aug. 25 on an agenda that called the deal “Project Osprey,” WWNO reported. Three residents and the Vermilion Citizens Coalition sued Oct. 26, saying the Police Jury and the board broke the Open Meetings Law eight times along the way.  Our story on the suit.  
 What are residents asking? 
 The citizens’ group Vermilion United wants a verbal SpaceX promise of fire equipment put on paper and is questioning where a $600,000-a-year administrative fee will go.  More here.  
 What is next door? 
 About 4,000 acres of Section 16 school land sits beside the site near White Lake. It could be swapped, but not sold without the Legislature’s OK, after an appraisal, Acadiana News First reported. 
 What comes next? 
  A judge has yet to schedule the open meetings suit.  The state’s cooperative endeavor agreement with SpaceX stays private until at least Dec. 14, according to Vermilion United.  Gov. Landry’s former chief of staff, Kyle Ruckert, is now registered to lobby for SpaceX, The Center Square reported.  
 The running timeline, numbers and open questions live on  Starbase Watch .

t: Citizen Group Presses for Answers on SpaceX Deal; Ex-Landry Aide Now a SpaceX Lobbyist
d: Vermilion United says the Starbase Louisiana tax agreement treats local hiring as a goal, not a promise, and wants a verbal SpaceX pledge on fire protection put in writing.
b:
A month-old Vermilion Parish citizens’ group says the paperwork behind Starbase Louisiana leaves residents with more hopes than guarantees, and it wants answers before construction starts. 
 Vermilion United came together days after Gov. Jeff Landry unveiled the SpaceX deal, organizer Melissa Hargrave told Acadiana News First in a report published Thursday. Since then the group has gotten hold of recordings from two meetings of the parish Industrial Development Board, held July 23 and Aug. 25, and it now posts transcripts online next to the text of the signed tax agreement so residents can compare what was said with what was signed. 
 “Our goal as a coalition is to make sure that we get as much information as possible so we can inform the public,” Hargrave told the station. 
 Three questions the group is pressing 
   Local jobs.  The payment-in-lieu-of-taxes agreement sets hiring targets, but the group says local hiring is written as a goal, not an obligation, so there is no promise the jobs go to parish residents.   A $600,000 fee.  The development board’s yearly administrative fee, capped at $600,000, is slated to go to One Acadiana, a privately run organization that promotes the wider Acadiana region. Hargrave argues the parish should keep it to restart its own economic development district. The station could not confirm whether that arrangement was ever approved, and One Acadiana was not available for an interview.   Fire protection.  In the recordings, the board’s lawyer says SpaceX verbally promised to supply firefighting equipment if the project lowers the parish’s fire rating, which could raise homeowners’ insurance. Hargrave wants that promise “codified in writing.” It is not in the signed tax agreement; it could be in the state’s separate cooperative endeavor agreement with SpaceX, which has not been made public. The group has requested that document from Louisiana Economic Development and was told it would come no sooner than Dec. 14.  
 A former Landry aide lobbies for SpaceX 
 Meanwhile, The Center Square reported that Kyle Ruckert, Landry’s chief of staff until February, is now registered to lobby for SpaceX, in a pay bracket of $100,000 to $249,000. Ruckert, who chairs the Landry-aligned nonprofit Protect Louisiana Values, could not be reached, the outlet said. 
 The same report puts the project’s promise at 3,000 direct jobs within ten years, paying $92,600 on average, with work starting in 2027 and a first launch aimed for 2029. 
 The citizens’ group is not the only challenge: three residents and the Vermilion Citizens Coalition have also sued to void the tax deal.  The Times reported on that suit Friday.

t: Kaplan Man Arrested on Drug and Firearm Charges After Search of Home
d: Investigators seized suspected methamphetamine, marijuana, prescription pills and two guns with an estimated street value of more than $68,000, KLFY reported.
b:
Police arrested a 43-year-old Kaplan man on drug and gun charges after neighbors’ complaints led investigators to a house on West Second Street, KLFY reported Thursday. 
 Officers said repeated complaints about suspected drug dealing at the home prompted weeks of surveillance and undercover work, followed by a search warrant, according to the station. 
 What was seized 
 Investigators listed the following, according to the report: 
   Suspected methamphetamine:  about 308 grams   Marijuana:  171 grams, plus 40 grams of synthetic marijuana   Prescription drugs:  170 cyclobenzaprine tablets, 11 clonazepam tablets, 11 Adderall tablets and half a Xanax tablet   Suboxone:  17 strips   Also:  two guns and drug paraphernalia  
 Authorities put the street value of the drugs at $68,055. Bond had not been set when the information was released, and the case is still under investigation, KLFY reported. 
 Charges are accusations, not convictions, and everyone arrested is presumed innocent unless proven guilty in court. The Times names people arrested only when the arresting agency releases the name and charges directly; KLFY’s report did not say which agency made the arrest.

t: Residents Sue to Void Parish’s SpaceX Tax Deal Over Open Meetings Law
d: A new citizens group and three residents say the Police Jury and a revived development board broke Louisiana’s Open Meetings Law eight times while approving the Starbase Louisiana agreement.
b:
Three Vermilion Parish residents and a newly formed citizens’ group have gone to court to undo the parish’s tax agreement with SpaceX, arguing that public officials approved it out of public view. 
 Filed Oct. 26 in the 15th Judicial District Court, the case targets two bodies: the Police Jury and the parish’s Industrial Development Board, WWNO and the Gulf States Newsroom reported. Bringing the case are the Vermilion Citizens Coalition and residents Cheryl Choate of Pecan Island, Rebecca C. Young and Dr. Robert J. Young III. 
 The complaint 
 The residents count eight breaches of Louisiana’s Open Meetings Law. The ones described in the reporting include: 
   No livestream.  The Police Jury’s July 15 and Aug. 19 meetings were not streamed online, as the suit says the law requires.   Thin notice.  Notices for the development board’s July 23 and Aug. 25 meetings were tacked to the courthouse door instead of going online or to the state commissioner of administration.   A code name.  The Aug. 25 agenda called the deal “Project Osprey” rather than describing it.   A mid-meeting revival.  The Police Jury revived the dormant development board on July 15 by changing its agenda during the meeting, which the plaintiffs call a “subterfuge.”  
 What they want 
 The plaintiffs ask a judge to throw out what the development board did on Aug. 25, when it approved the payment-in-lieu-of-taxes deal, so the vote would have to happen again in the open. 
 The money in play 
 Under the deal, SpaceX’s yearly payments to the parish begin at $25 million and grow 2% annually over a 25-year term. The Gulf States Newsroom totals that at about $800 million, against a property tax break it values at close to $23.8 billion over the same stretch. 
 The responses 
 Plaintiffs’ attorney William Most of New Orleans said the law exists to “make sure that our public officials are working for us, not the other way around,” WWNO reported. 
 The Police Jury declined to comment and the development board did not respond, according to the station. The board’s own minutes state the Aug. 25 notice was “duly posted and given in the manner provided by the Open Meetings Law.” The governor’s office said its executive counsel was present on July 15 and that the settlement was discussed in closed session before a public vote. SpaceX did not respond. 
 No court date had been reported as of Friday. 
 Nearby: school land 
 In a separate development, Acadiana News First reported Oct. 28 that the parish school district holds roughly 4,000 acres of Section 16 education land beside the planned spaceport near White Lake. That kind of land can be traded but not sold without the Legislature’s approval, and an appraisal would come before any talks. “Basically, we have to look at that land,” Superintendent Tommy Byler told the station. 
 The Times will follow both stories on  Starbase Watch .

t: What’s on the Ballot in Vermilion Parish on Tuesday
d: Contested races for district attorney, mayor of Erath and Gueydan, two School Board seats and more are on the Nov. 3 ballot, along with 10 statewide constitutional amendments.
b:
Vermilion Parish voters go to the polls Tuesday, Nov. 3, to choose a U.S. senator and congressman, a district attorney, two mayors, two School Board members and a long list of local officers, according to the Louisiana Secretary of State’s candidate list for the parish. Ten proposed amendments to the state constitution are also on every ballot. 
 Many local offices drew only one candidate when qualifying closed in August, and those candidates are elected without appearing on the ballot. The contested races are below. 
 Federal races 
 For  U.S. Senate , “Jamie” Davis, a Democrat, faces Julia Letlow, a Republican. 
 Six candidates are running for  U.S. Representative, 3rd Congressional District : “Kate” Cotten (Republican), John Day (Democrat), Priscilla Gonzalez (Democrat), “Clay” Higgins (Republican), Tia LeBrun (No Party) and Caleb “With a C” Walker (Democrat). 
 District attorney and courts 
 Two Republicans are running for  district attorney of the 15th Judicial District , which includes Vermilion Parish: Kristian Earles and Donald “Don” Landry. 
 In Kaplan, William J. Seaux and Ruby Thibeaux, both Republicans, are running for  Kaplan City Marshal . 
 Five court races drew a single candidate: “Tommy” Frederick and Laurie Hulin for 15th Judicial District Court judge (Divisions C and G), Richard Putnam III for Abbeville city judge, Stanton Hardee III for Kaplan city judge and Jeremiah Bolden for Abbeville city marshal. 
 School Board 
 Two of the nine School Board seats are contested: 
   District C:  Harry “Gregg” Meaux (No Party) and Coeyn Wise (No Party).   District F:  Tyrone Alexander (Democrat) and Roderick Darby (No Party).  
 Unopposed candidates in the other seven districts are David Dupuis (A), Kevin Meyers (B), “Dale” Stelly (D), Charlotte C. Detraz (E), Jason Roy (G), “Chris” Hebert (H) and “Nick” Touchet (I). 
 Towns and city 
   Mayor of Erath:  Stephanie P. Broussard (No Party) and Marlene Menard (Republican).   Mayor of Gueydan:  Jeffrey Lamson (No Party), Efrem “Zim” Livingston (Democrat) and Jason Suire (Republican).   Erath chief of police:  Anna Lapointe (No Party) and Randall Toups (Republican).   Maurice chief of police:  John Dayries and Guy Nerren, both Republicans.   Gueydan aldermen:  seven candidates for five seats.   Maurice aldermen:  six candidates for five seats.   Abbeville City Council, District A:  Cornelius Darby (Democrat) and William “Billy” Noegel (No Party).  
 Neil Arsement, the only candidate for mayor of Maurice, and Cru Delcambre, the only candidate for Gueydan police chief, were unopposed, and five candidates qualified for Erath’s five aldermen seats. 
 Justice of the peace 
 In Ward 4, Philip DeBaillon and Cheryl Granger, both Republicans, are running for  justice of the peace . Candidates for justice of the peace and constable in the parish’s other wards were unopposed. 
 Ten constitutional amendments 
 Statewide, voters will decide 10 proposed constitutional amendments. According to the ballot language published by the Secretary of State, they include: 
  letting the surviving spouse of a veteran with a service-connected disability keep a property tax exemption (Amendment 1);  barring post-conviction bail for a defendant convicted of an aggravated offense against a minor child (Amendment 3);  barring anyone who has served more than one and one-half terms as governor from being elected governor again (Amendment 4);  prohibiting expropriation of property by a foreign adversary (Amendment 8).  
 The full text of all 10 is on the Secretary of State’s website. 
 Before you go 
 Voters can look up their polling place, hours and a sample ballot on the Secretary of State’s Voter Portal at voterportal.sos.la.gov or in the GeauxVote mobile app. 
 The Vermilion Parish Police Jury office will be closed Monday, Nov. 2, for All Saints Day and Tuesday, Nov. 3, for Election Day, according to a notice on the Police Jury’s website. 
 The Times will report Vermilion Parish results after the polls
